title: Chapter 6: Hypothesis Tests
text:
What you’ll learn
By the end of Chapter 6 you’ll be able to:

State null and alternative hypotheses for one-sided and two-sided tests.
Compute and interpret p-values using \(Z\), \(t\), \(\chi^2\), and \(F\) reference distributions.
Run one-sample tests for a population mean, proportion, and variance.
Run two-sample tests for differences in means, differences in proportions, and ratios of variances.
Recognize when paired data should be tested through differences.
Write conclusions in context without overclaiming what a p-value means.

title: Chapter 6: Hypothesis Tests
text:
Key ideas

Hypothesis Test Logic
A hypothesis test asks whether the observed sample statistic would be unusual if the null hypothesis were true. Small p-values give evidence against the null hypothesis.


P-Value Interpretation
The p-value is calculated assuming \(H_0\) is true. It is not the probability that \(H_0\) is true, and failing to reject \(H_0\) does not prove \(H_0\).


One-Sample Tests
Use a one-sample \(z\) test when \(\sigma\) is known, a one-sample \(t\) test when \(\sigma\) is unknown, a one-proportion \(z\) test for a population proportion, and a chi-square test for a population variance.


Two-Sample Tests
For independent groups, test differences such as \(\mu_1-\mu_2\) or \(p_1-p_2\). For paired data, first compute differences within each pair and then run a one-sample \(t\) test on \(\mu_d\).


Choosing the Right Reference Distribution
The reference distribution comes from the parameter and what is known: \(Z\) for known standard deviations or large-count proportion tests, \(t\) for unknown standard deviations, \(\chi^2\) for one variance, and \(F\) for a ratio of variances.

title: Chapter 5: Confidence Intervals
text:
What you’ll learn
By the end of Chapter 5 you’ll be able to:

Explain the difference between a point estimate and a confidence interval.
Interpret confidence intervals using correct repeated-sampling language.
Construct one-sample confidence intervals for a mean when \(\sigma\) is known and when \(\sigma\) is unknown.
Construct confidence intervals for a population proportion and a population variance.
Construct two-sample confidence intervals for differences in means, differences in proportions, and ratios of variances.
Recognize when paired data should be reduced to one sample of differences.
Choose a sample size that achieves a desired margin of error.

title: Chapter 5: Confidence Intervals
text:
Key ideas

Confidence Interval Skeleton
Most confidence intervals follow the same pattern: \[
\text{estimate} \pm
\left(\text{critical value}\right)
\left(\text{standard error}\right).
\] The critical value comes from a reference distribution such as \(Z\), \(t\), \(\chi^2\), or \(F\).


Interpretation
A 95% confidence interval does not mean there is a 95% probability that this particular interval contains the parameter. The parameter is fixed. Instead, the method captures the true parameter in about 95% of repeated samples.


One-Sample Intervals
Use a \(z\)-interval when estimating a mean with known \(\sigma\), a \(t\)-interval when \(\sigma\) is unknown, a normal approximation for a proportion when success-failure counts are large, and a chi-square interval for a variance when the population is normal.


Two-Sample Intervals
For independent groups, the target parameter is usually a difference: \(\mu_1-\mu_2\) or \(p_1-p_2\). For paired data, first compute differences within each pair, then build a one-sample \(t\)-interval for \(\mu_d\).


Planning Sample Size
To guarantee a margin of error \(E\), solve the margin-of-error formula for \(n\) and always round up. For proportions with no prior estimate, use the conservative planning value \(p^*=0.5\).

title: Chapter 2: An Introduction to R
text:
What you’ll learn
By the end of Chapter 2 you’ll be able to:

Explain why we use R rather than point-and-click software, and tell R apart from RStudio.
Install R and RStudio and navigate the four main panes of the IDE.
Use R as a calculator — arithmetic, exponents, logs, and built-in math functions.
Create and work with the core R data structures: vectors, lists, matrices, arrays, factors, and data frames.
Call built-in functions like mean(), sd(), hist() and read their output.
Install and load packages with install.packages() and library().

title: Chapter 2: An Introduction to R
text:
Key ideas

R vs RStudio
R is the engine that runs the calculations. RStudio is the dashboard you use to drive it. You install R first, then RStudio on top of it.


Scripts beat point-and-click
Writing analysis as code makes it reproducible, easy to share, and easy to re-run when the data changes. This is the single biggest reason statisticians use R.


R as a calculator
R handles + - * /, exponentiation ^, modulo %%, integer division %/%, and a full set of math functions (sqrt, log, exp, abs, round) and trig functions out of the box.


Data structures

Vectors — same-type values in one dimension
Lists — mixed types, any structure
Matrices / Arrays — same type, 2+ dimensions
Factors — categorical variables with named levels
Data frames — table of variables (columns) and observations (rows)



Functions and packages
Most R commands look like function_name(input). Packages extend R with new functions — install once with install.packages(), load each session with library().

title: STA258
text:
3.1 Representing Data

Data and notation
Data are measurements we write symbolically. For \(n\) observations, we use a lowercase letter \(x\) with a subscript for the index:
\[x_1, \; x_2, \; \ldots, \; x_n\]
where \(x_i\) is one observation and \(i = 1, \ldots, n\). The value \(n\) is the sample size.



Condensed form: \(\; x_i : i = 1, \ldots, n\)

title: STA258
text:
3.1 Tabular Form





Index
1
2
\(\cdots\)
\(n\)




Observation
\(x_1\)
\(x_2\)
\(\cdots\)
\(x_n\)





Example. Five students’ study hours:
\[3, \; 4, \; 4, \; 6, \; 8\]
Here \(n = 5\), \(x_1 = 3\), \(x_2 = 4\), \(\ldots\), \(x_5 = 8\).




Why bother with notation?
Once we write data as \(x_1, \ldots, x_n\), every formula in this chapter (mean, variance, IQR) reads the same regardless of what the data actually measure.

title: STA258
text:
3.2 Numerical Measures


Centre Where is the “typical” value? Mean, median, mode.


Spread How dispersed are the values? Variance, SD, range, IQR.


Position Where does one value sit relative to the rest? Percentiles, quartiles.




No single number tells the whole story. We pair centre with spread, and read both alongside a plot.

title: STA258
text:
3.2.1 Mean



Sample mean \(\bar{x}\)
For a sample \(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n\),
\[\bar{x} \; = \; \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i}{n} \; = \; \frac{x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n}{n}\]


The mean is the arithmetic average - the one most people mean when they say “average.”

title: STA258
text:
3.2.2 Median

Median
The middle value of a data set once the observations are sorted in ascending order.
Let \(x_{(1)}, x_{(2)}, \ldots, x_{(n)}\) be the sorted values. Then:

If \(n\) is odd: \(\;\;\) Median \(=\) observation \(\left(\dfrac{n+1}{2}\right)\)
If \(n\) is even: \(\;\;\) Median \(=\) average of observations \(\left(\dfrac{n}{2}\right)\) and \(\left(\dfrac{n}{2} + 1\right)\)

title: STA258
text:
3.2.2 Median in R













Sorted odd: 1, 1, 3, 4, 5 → middle value is 3.
Sorted even: 1, 1, 3, 4, 5, 9 → middle pair is 3 and 4, so median \(= (3 + 4)/2 = 3.5\).

title: STA258
text:
3.2.3 Mode



Mode
The most frequently occurring value in a data set.
A data set can be unimodal, bimodal, or have no mode if every value appears the same number of times.

text:

\[2, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 7, 7, 9, 12\]
(a) Find the mean study time.
(b) Find the median study time.
(c) Find the mode.

title: STA258
text:
3.2.4 Variance



Sample variance \(s^2\)
The average squared deviation from the mean:
\[s^{2} \; = \; \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}\]
where \(\bar{x}\) is the sample mean.




Each term is squared, so \(s^2 \ge 0\) always.
The units of \(s^2\) are the units of the data squared (e.g. dollars²). That is awkward to interpret, which is why we usually report the standard deviation instead.

title: STA258
text:
Why divide by \(n-1\)?

Bessel’s correction. We use sample data \(\bar{x}\) to estimate the (unknown) population mean \(\mu\). That estimation step “uses up” one piece of information.
Dividing by \(n - 1\) instead of \(n\) corrects for this, and makes \(s^2\) an unbiased estimator of the population variance.


You will see a formal proof of this in STA260. For now, just remember:

Sample variance → divide by \(n - 1\)
Population variance → divide by \(N\)

title: STA258
text:
3.2.4 Variance in R













Tip. Build the table \((x_i, x_i - \bar{x}, (x_i - \bar{x})^2)\) on paper before reaching for var(). Several exam questions ask for the table.

title: STA258
text:
3.2.5 Standard Deviation



Sample standard deviation \(s\)
\[s \; = \; +\sqrt{s^{2}}\]
where \(s^2\) is the sample variance.


Taking the square root returns us to the original units, which is why we usually report \(s\) rather than \(s^2\).

title: STA258
text:
3.2.6 Range



Range
\[\text{Range} \; = \; \max(x_1, \ldots, x_n) \; - \; \min(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\]
The difference between the largest and smallest observations.


Caution. The range uses only two values, so a single extreme observation can change it dramatically. It is a quick summary, not a robust one.

title: STA258
text:
3.2.7 Percentiles

\(p^{\text{th}}\) percentile
In an ordered data set, the \(p^{\text{th}}\) percentile is the value such that \(p\%\) of all observations lie below it.


Example. A class writes a difficult test and a student scores 72%. Although 72% is a B-, the test was hard. In fact, this mark sits at the 90th percentile for this test - the student scored higher than 90% of the class.
A relative position can matter more than the raw mark.

title: STA258
text:
3.2.8 Quartiles

Quartiles
Three values that split the sorted data into four equal-size groups.

First quartile \(Q_1\): 25% of values below it.
Second quartile \(Q_2\): 50% of values below it. This is the median.
Third quartile \(Q_3\): 75% of values below it.



Quartiles are just three specific percentiles: \(Q_1 = P_{25}\), \(Q_2 = P_{50}\), \(Q_3 = P_{75}\).

title: STA258
text:
Interquartile Range (IQR)



IQR
\[\text{IQR} \; = \; Q_3 - Q_1\]
The width of the middle 50% of the data.


Unlike the range, the IQR is resistant to outliers because the bottom 25% and top 25% of the data are ignored.

title: STA258
text:

\[52, 58, 61, 65, 70, 72, 75, 78, 82, 86, 90, 96\]
(a) Find the median.
(b) Find the first quartile, \(Q_{1}\).
(c) Find the third quartile, \(Q_{3}\).
(d) Find the interquartile range (IQR).
(e) Using the \(1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) rule, which scores would be flagged as unusually low or high?

title: STA258
text:
3.3 Graphical Techniques


Why plot at all? Numbers alone hide the shape of a distribution. A picture reveals skewness, gaps, clusters, and unusual values.


Two workhorses Histograms show the full shape of one variable. Boxplots highlight centre, spread, and outliers, and stack neatly for group comparisons.




Pair numbers with pictures. A mean of 65 looks different on a symmetric bell than on a right-skewed pile with a long tail. Always look at both.

title: STA258
text:
Skewness

Skewness
A measure of the symmetry (or lack of it) in the distribution of data.



Left-skewed Long tail on the left. Most values bunched on the right. Also called negatively skewed.


Symmetric Roughly mirror-image around the centre. Mean \(\approx\) median.


Right-skewed Long tail on the right. Most values bunched on the left. Also called positively skewed.

title: STA258
text:
Skewness Illustrated


The tail points in the direction of the skew. “Right-skewed” = tail to the right. The mean is pulled toward the tail; the median stays near the bulk.

title: STA258
text:
Skewness vs Mean & Median



Rule of thumb

Left-skewed: Mean \(<\) Median
Symmetric: Mean \(\approx\) Median
Right-skewed: Mean \(>\) Median

The mean is pulled toward the long tail. The median is not.

title: STA258
text:
Outliers



Outlier
A data point that appears to lie outside the overall pattern of the rest of the data.


Do not just delete outliers.
Investigate first - is it a data-entry error, a measurement error, or a genuine rare observation? The right call depends on the cause.




Common causes

Transcription error (typing 100 instead of 10)
Measurement error (broken instrument)
A real but unusual case (a millionaire in a sample of incomes)

title: STA258
text:
3.3.1 Histograms

Histogram
A plot of a quantitative variable, built by:

Splitting the range of the data into intervals (bins).
Counting how many observations fall in each bin.
Drawing a bar over each bin with height equal to its frequency.

The \(x\)-axis shows the bins, and the \(y\)-axis shows frequency (or relative frequency).


Frequency vs relative frequency. Frequency histograms show raw counts; relative-frequency histograms show proportions (each bar height \(= f_i / F\), where \(F = \sum f_i\)).

title: STA258
text:
3.3.2 Boxplots

Boxplot (box-and-whisker plot)
A five-number summary in graphical form:

Box spans from \(Q_1\) to \(Q_3\).
Line inside the box marks the median.
Whiskers extend out to the most extreme observation inside the outlier cutoffs.
Dots beyond the whiskers are flagged as potential outliers.

title: STA258
text:
The \(1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) Rule



Outlier cutoffs (fences)
\[\text{Lower cutoff} = Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\] \[\text{Upper cutoff} = Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\]
Any value outside these cutoffs is flagged as a potential outlier.




Example. A dataset has \(Q_1 = 5\), \(Q_3 = 11\), so \(\text{IQR} = 6\) and \(1.5 \times \text{IQR} = 9\).

Lower cutoff: \(5 - 9 = -4\)
Upper cutoff: \(11 + 9 = 20\)

Any value below \(-4\) or above \(20\) would be flagged.

title: STA258
text:
3.3.2 Boxplot in R













What to look for

Where does the median sit inside the box? Off-centre suggests skew.
How long are the whiskers? Unequal whisker lengths also suggest skew.
Any dots? Those are potential outliers.

title: STA258
text:
Skewness from a Boxplot


Reading skew from a box. Median closer to \(Q_3\) + long lower whisker → left skew. Median closer to \(Q_1\) + long upper whisker → right skew. The longer tail points in the direction of the skew.

Centre Mean uses every value. Median ignores extremes. Mode is the most common value.

title: STA258
text:
The Big Question

How can we say something true aboutmillions of people we’ve never met?




Pollsters call ~1,000 Canadians and predict an election for 40 million. Doctors test a drug on 500 patients and recommend it for everyone. Netflix watches a sample of users and decides what shows to make.




That gap between “what we measured” and “what we want to know” - that’s what this whole course is about.

title: STA258
text:
Roadmap


1 - Foundations Statistics, population, sample, unit, observation, variable, and the difference between descriptive and inferential ideas.


2 - Types of Data Quantitative vs qualitative data, plus discrete vs continuous and nominal vs ordinal categories.


3 - Inference Preview Sampling, bias, study types, and the first ideas behind drawing conclusions from data.





Core skill Thinking carefully about what data represent before you compute anything.


Core tool Vocabulary like population, sample, parameter, statistic, and variable.


Core habit Match every numerical claim with the correct data context.

title: STA258
text:
1.1 Foundations

Definition 1.1 - Statistics The science of collecting, classifying, summarizing, analyzing, and interpreting data.




Think of statistics as a pipeline:  Question → Data → Analysis → Decision


The five verbs in the definition map roughly to the chapters of the course.

title: STA258
text:
Population

Definition 1.2 - Population The entire group of individuals, items, or measurements that share a characteristic of interest and about which conclusions are to be drawn.



Examples:

All students at the University of Toronto
All residents of Mississauga
Every possible hand in a game of poker (hypothetical!)
Every battery a factory will ever produce





A population can be real or hypothetical, finite or essentially infinite. What matters is that it’s the group you actually want to learn about.

title: STA258
text:
Sample

Definition 1.3 - Sample A subset selected from the population.


Examples:

50 randomly selected U of T students
100 randomly selected Mississauga residents
30 batteries pulled off the production line today




Why sample? Measuring everyone is usually too slow, too expensive, or simply impossible.

title: STA258
text:
Visualizing Population vs Sample







Hover over any dot to see which unit it is. Grey = population, teal = the sample.

title: STA258
text:
Your Turn: Identify Them

A researcher wants to know the average sleep of all UTM students. She randomly surveys 200 UTM students and finds they sleep 6.8 hours on average.  What is the population? What is the sample?



Population: All UTM students. Sample: The 200 surveyed UTM students.


Pause and have students answer aloud before revealing.

title: STA258
text:
Unit, Observation, Variable

Unit - the smallest entity from which data are collected (one row).


Observation - the full set of measured values for one unit.


Variable - a characteristic that varies from unit to unit (one column).

title: STA258
text:
Population Unit vs Sample Unit



Population unit One member of the entire population.


One U of T student, when the population is all U of T students.



Sample unit One member of the selected sample.


One of the 50 students you actually surveyed.




Every sample unit is also a population unit - but not the other way around.

title: STA258
text:
Parameter vs Statistic



Parameter A number that describes the population. Usually unknown.



Statistic A number that describes the sample. Calculated from data - known.




Memory trick:   Parameter ↔︎ Population  |  Statistic ↔︎ Sample  (both start with the same letter).

title: STA258
text:
Descriptive vs Inferential Statistics

Descriptive statistics Numerical and graphical methods used to summarize the data you have.


Inferential statistics Using a sample to generalize to a larger population.

title: STA258
text:
Spot the Difference


Descriptive

“The average mark in this lecture of 80 students is 72%.”  “63% of these 400 Torontonians support the plan.”


Inferential

“We estimate the average STA258 mark across all sections is around 72%.”  “We estimate ~63% of all Toronto residents support the plan.”




Tell: descriptive describes this data. Inferential makes a claim beyond the data.

title: STA258
text:
1.2 Types of Data

Quantitative data Numerical measurements where arithmetic is meaningful.


Qualitative (categorical) data Values fall into categories; arithmetic doesn’t make sense.



Trap: a number doesn’t automatically mean quantitative. Postal codes, jersey numbers, and student IDs look numeric but are categorical.

Continuous Any value in a range; measured on a scale.



Height
Time spent studying
Temperature

Nominal Categories with no natural order.



Eye colour
Program of study
Primary device (phone/laptop/tablet)




Ordinal Categories with a natural order.



Self-rated health (Poor → Excellent)
Movie rating (1–5 stars)
Education level

title: STA258
text: 1.3 Introduction to Inferential Statistics

title: STA258
text:
Why Uncertainty Is Built In

Two different samples of 100 UTM students will give two different sample means. So any estimate must come with a measure of how much it might be off.



This is where the tools in later chapters come from:

Confidence intervals - a range of plausible parameter values
Hypothesis tests - checking whether data support a specific claim
Statistical power - how likely we are to detect a real effect

title: STA258
text:
See Sampling Variability









Run it 5 times. Notice the sample mean changes each time - even though the true population mean is exactly 70.

title: STA258
text:
A Closer Look at Sampling
How you collect your sample determines whether inference is honest.

Simple random sample (SRS) - every unit has an equal chance of being chosen.


Systematic - every \(k\)-th unit from an ordered list (e.g., every 50th student).


Stratified - divide into groups, sample from each group.


Cluster - randomly pick whole groups, survey everyone inside.


Convenience / Voluntary response - whoever is easy to reach or chooses to respond. ⚠ Usually biased.

title: STA258
text:
Bias: When Samples Lie

Bias - a systematic tendency for a sample to differ from the population in a particular direction.




Classic bias traps:

Selection bias - surveying gym-goers about exercise habits
Voluntary response - Instagram polls (only loud opinions answer)
Non-response bias - the people who skip the survey are different from those who answer
Coverage bias - your sampling frame misses parts of the population

title: STA258
text:
Exercise: Identify the Bias

For each scenario, identify the type of bias present and explain why it is a problem. We will discuss in class.


The Office of the Registrar wants to estimate the average GPA of all undergraduates. They collect data by emailing only students who belong to an academic club.
A student newspaper posts an online poll asking “How satisfied are you with library hours?” and reports the results as representative of all students.
A course evaluation survey is sent to a random sample of 1,000 students, but only 200 respond.
A study on student commuting habits recruits participants by posting flyers only in on-campus residence buildings.
A survey asks students to self-report how many hours per week they spend studying.

title: STA258
text:
Observational vs Experimental Studies



Observational Record what’s already happening - no intervention.


Survey adults: do you take vitamins? Did you catch a cold?



Experimental Randomly assign participants to treatments, then compare.


Randomly give half the volunteers Vitamin C, half a placebo, and compare cold rates.




Only well-designed experiments can establish cause and effect.

title: STA258
text:
Exercise: Types of Studies

Classify each as an observational study, experimental study, or sample survey. Briefly justify your answer. We will take these up in class.


A researcher records the GPA and weekly study hours of students in STA258 without intervening, to see whether there is an association between the two.
First-year students are randomly assigned to either a weekly tutoring program or no tutoring. Their final exam grades are compared at the end of term.
At the end of the semester, a random sample of students is emailed a questionnaire asking about teaching quality, workload, and course organization.
A study tracks whether students who commute more than 1 hour to campus report higher stress levels than those who live on campus.
Students are randomly given one of two versions of a course syllabus (one with weekly deadlines, one with monthly deadlines) and their assignment submission rates are recorded.

title: STA258
text:
Chapter 1 Summary



Statistics = science of learning from data under uncertainty.


We study a sample to learn about a population.


Parameters describe populations (unknown); statistics describe samples (known).


Data are quantitative (discrete/continuous) or qualitative (nominal/ordinal).


Inference uses a sample statistic to estimate an unknown population parameter - with a measure of uncertainty.


How we sample (and whether we experiment) determines whether inference is trustworthy.

title: STA258
text:
Chapter Roadmap


5.3 - One Sample Means, proportions, and variances. Decide between \(Z\), \(t\), and \(\chi^2\).


5.4 - Two Sample Differences in means, differences in proportions, and ratios of variances.


5.6 - Planning Choose \(n\) so a confidence interval reaches a target margin of error.





Core skill Identify the parameter before choosing the formula.


Core tool Use qnorm(), qt(), qchisq(), and qf() for critical values.


Core habit Interpret the interval in context, with units.

title: STA258
text:
5.1 Point Estimates and Interval Estimates


Point estimate
A single numerical value computed from sample data that serves as the best guess of an unknown population parameter.
Examples: \(\bar{x}\) estimates \(\mu\), \(s^2\) estimates \(\sigma^2\), and \(\hat p\) estimates \(p\).


Confidence interval
A plausible range of values for a population parameter, built from sample data and a specified confidence level.



Big idea. A statistic will usually not equal the parameter exactly. The interval tells us how far away the statistic could reasonably be.

title: STA258
text:
The CI Skeleton

Most confidence intervals (means, proportions, and their differences) follow the symmetric form:
\[
\text{estimate} \pm
\underbrace{(\text{critical value})(\text{standard error})}_{\text{margin of error}}
\]


Intervals for a variance \(\sigma^2\) follow their own skeleton — an asymmetric one built directly from the \(\chi^2\) distribution:
\[
\left(
\frac{\text{estimate}}{\text{upper critical value}},\
\frac{\text{estimate}}{\text{lower critical value}}
\right)
\quad\text{where estimate} = (n-1)s^2
\]



Estimate \(\bar{x}\), \(\hat p\), \(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2\), or \(\hat p_1-\hat p_2\).


Critical value From \(Z\) or \(t\), depending on the sampling distribution.


Standard error The standard deviation of the estimator, or an estimate of it.

title: STA258
text:
5.2 Interpreting Confidence



For a \(C\%\) confidence interval:
In repeated sampling, about \(C\%\) of intervals constructed using this method will capture the true parameter.


Do not say: “There is a 95% probability that this particular interval contains \(\mu\).”
The parameter is fixed. The random object is the interval produced by the sample.

title: STA258
text:
5.3.1.1 One Mean, Known \(\sigma\)

When the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is known:
\[
\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}
\]
Use this for a population mean \(\mu\) with known \(\sigma\).



Assumptions


Random sample or randomized experiment.


Independent observations.


Population is normal, or \(n\) is large enough for the CLT.




Exam cue If the problem gives a population standard deviation, use \(z\). If it gives a sample standard deviation, use \(t\).

text:
Example: Known Sigma - Magazine Readers

Playbill magazine reports \(\bar{x}=119{,}155\) dollars from \(n=80\) households. Assume \(\sigma=30{,}000\) dollars.
Construct 90%, 95%, and 99% confidence intervals for the population mean household income of readers.










Level
Critical value
Margin of error
Confidence interval




90%
1.645
\(1.645(30000/\sqrt{80})=5517.38\)

95%
1.960
\(1.960(30000/\sqrt{80})=6573.04\)
\((112581.96, 125728.04)\)


99%
2.576
\(2.576(30000/\sqrt{80})=8640.41\)
\((110514.59, 127795.41)\)

text:
Example: Known Sigma - Car Sales



Annual car sales are normally distributed with known \(\sigma=15\). For a random sample of 15 salespeople:
\[79,43,58,66,101,63,79,33,58,71,60,101,74,55,88\]
Construct a 95% CI for \(\mu\).














\(\bar{x}=68.6\), so the interval is approximately \((61.01, 76.19)\). We are 95% confident that the population mean number of cars sold annually is between about 61 and 76.

Question

title: STA258
text:
5.3.1.2 One Mean, Unknown \(\sigma\)

When \(\sigma\) is unknown, estimate it with \(s\) and use the Student \(t\) distribution:
\[
\bar{x} \pm t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\frac{s}{\sqrt n}
\]



Why t? Replacing \(\sigma\) with \(s\) adds uncertainty. The \(t\) distribution has heavier tails, especially for small degrees of freedom.


Small samples For small \(n\), check that the population is reasonably normal or that the sample has no severe skew/outliers.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Unknown Sigma - Ancient Air



Nitrogen percentages from air bubbles trapped in ancient amber:
\[63.4,65.0,64.4,63.3,54.8,64.5,60.8,49.1,51.0\]
Construct a 90% CI for the mean nitrogen percentage.


Using \(n=9\), \(\bar{x}=59.5889\), \(s=6.2553\), and \(t^*=1.8595\):
\[59.5889\pm1.8595\frac{6.2553}{3}=(55.71,63.47).\]

title: STA258
text:
Example: Unknown Sigma - Camera Photos



A random sample of 10 digital camera owners has stored photo counts:
\[25,6,22,26,31,18,13,20,14,2\]
Construct a 95% CI for the population mean number of stored photos.














\(\bar{x}=17.7\), \(s=9.0805\), \(df=9\), and \(t^*=2.262\). The 95% CI is approximately \((11.20,24.20)\) photos.

title: STA258
text:
5.3.2 One Proportion

For a population proportion \(p\), with \(\hat p=x/n\):
\[
\hat p \pm z_{\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}
\]



Conditions


Random sample.


Independent Bernoulli trials.


Sufficiently large counts: \(n\hat p \ge 10\) and \(n(1-\hat p)\ge 10\).




Boundary check The final interval should make sense for a proportion. Values below 0 or above 1 need careful handling.

title: STA258
text:
Example: One Proportion - Transit Use

A UTM survey asks 1200 students whether they commute on MiWay transit. Among them, 738 say yes.
Construct a 95% CI for the true proportion of students who commute on MiWay.



\[\hat p=\frac{738}{1200}=0.6150\]
\[SE=\sqrt{\frac{0.6150(0.3850)}{1200}}=0.01405\]


\[\hat p \pm z_{\alpha/2}\,SE\]
\[=0.6150\pm1.96(0.01405)\]
\[=(0.5875,\,0.6425)\]



We are 95% confident that between 58.75% and 64.25% of UTM students commute on MiWay.

title: STA258
section: Example: One Proportion - Work From Home
text:
Example: One Proportion - Work From Home



At the software firm Northwind, a survey of 650 employees finds 286 prefer working from home at least three days per week.
Construct a 90% CI for the population proportion.














\(\hat p=0.44\), so the 90% CI is approximately \((0.4079,0.4721)\).

title: STA258
text:
Question


For a one-proportion confidence interval, which sample has enough successes and failures for the normal approximation?




\(n=20\), \(\hat p=0.90\)
\(n=50\), \(\hat p=0.10\)
\(n=100\), \(\hat p=0.20\)
\(n=15\), \(\hat p=0.50\)

title: STA258
text:
5.3.3 One Variance

For a normally distributed population, a confidence interval for \(\sigma^2\) is:
\[
\left(
\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{\alpha/2,n-1}},
\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_{1-\alpha/2,n-1}}
\right)
\]


This interval is asymmetric. Normality matters here much more than it does for large-sample mean intervals.

title: STA258
text:
Example: One Variance - Bottle Filling

A random sample of 25 bottles from the kombucha brand Fizz has sample variance \(s^2=12.5\) (mL\(^2\)). Consistency matters here: customers notice when fill levels vary. Assume filling amounts are normally distributed.
Construct a 95% CI for \(\sigma^2\).

\[df=24,\quad \chi^2_{0.975,24}=39.364,\quad \chi^2_{0.025,24}=12.401\]
\[
\text{Lower}=\frac{24(12.5)}{39.364}=7.62,\qquad
\text{Upper}=\frac{24(12.5)}{12.401}=24.19
\]

The 95% CI for the population variance is approximately \((7.62,24.19)\).

title: STA258
text:
Example: One Variance - Reaction Times



Human reaction time to a visual signal averages about a quarter of a second — a well-established result in psychology. A random sample of 16 drivers tested in a driving simulator has sample variance \(s^2=0.36\) (seconds\(^2\)). Assume reaction times are normally distributed.
Construct a 90% CI for \(\sigma^2\).














The 90% CI is approximately \((0.2160,0.7437)\).

title: STA258
text:
5.4.1.1 Two Means: Known \(\sigma_1,\sigma_2\)

When both population standard deviations are known:
\[
(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)\pm z_{\alpha/2}
\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}}
\]


Reality check This case is uncommon in practice because population standard deviations are rarely known. We will use two short worked examples, then focus on the more realistic \(t\) intervals.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Known Sigmas - Course Marks

Suppose final marks in the same course are compared between two campuses.
UTSG: \(n_1=64\), \(\bar{x}_1=76\), known \(\sigma_1=10\).
UTM: \(n_2=81\), \(\bar{x}_2=72\), known \(\sigma_2=12\).
Construct a 95% CI for \(\mu_1-\mu_2\).

\[
\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2=4
\]
\[
SE=\sqrt{\frac{10^2}{64}+\frac{12^2}{81}}=1.827
\]
\[
4\pm1.96(1.827)=(0.42,7.58)
\]

We are 95% confident that the UTSG population mean is between 0.42 and 7.58 marks higher than the UTM population mean.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Known Sigmas - Study Time

Two independent samples compare average weekly study time.
Group 1: \(n_1=40\), \(\bar{x}_1=12.4\), known \(\sigma_1=3.2\).
Group 2: \(n_2=35\), \(\bar{x}_2=10.9\), known \(\sigma_2=2.8\).
Construct a 95% CI for \(\mu_1-\mu_2\).










The 95% CI is approximately \((0.14,2.86)\) hours. Group 1 appears to study more hours per week on average.

title: STA258
text:
5.4.1.3 Two Means: Equal Variances

If the two population variances are unknown but assumed equal:
\[
(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)\pm t_{n_1+n_2-2,\alpha/2}
s_p\sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1}+\frac{1}{n_2}}
\]
where
\[
s_p^2=\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2}.
\]

title: STA258
text:
Example: Pooled t - Battery Brands

A researcher compares battery life for two brands of the same device.
Brand A: \(n_1=12\), \(\bar{x}_1=52.4\), \(s_1=6.1\).
Brand B: \(n_2=10\), \(\bar{x}_2=47.8\), \(s_2=5.4\).
Assume equal population variances. Construct a 95% CI for \(\mu_1-\mu_2\).

\[
s_p^2=\frac{11(6.1^2)+9(5.4^2)}{20}=33.493,\quad s_p=5.787
\]
\[
SE=5.787\sqrt{\frac{1}{12}+\frac{1}{10}}=2.476,\quad t^*_{20}=2.086
\]
\[
4.6\pm2.086(2.476)=(-0.57,9.77)
\]

Because the interval contains 0, the data do not clearly show a nonzero mean battery-life difference.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Pooled t - Tutorial Methods



Method A: \(n_1=15\), \(\bar{x}_1=84.2\), \(s_1=7.5\).
Method B: \(n_2=14\), \(\bar{x}_2=78.6\), \(s_2=6.8\).
Assume equal variances. Construct a 90% CI for \(\mu_1-\mu_2\).














The 90% CI is approximately \((1.06,10.14)\) points. Method A appears to have a higher mean quiz score.

title: STA258
text:
5.4.1.4 Two Means: Unequal Variances

For unequal unknown variances, use Welch’s interval:
\[
(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)\pm t_{df,\alpha/2}
\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1}+\frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}.
\]


Degrees of freedom Software uses the Welch-Satterthwaite approximation. A conservative hand approximation is \(df=\min(n_1-1,n_2-1)\).

title: STA258
STA258
text:
Example: Welch t - Commute Times

Group 1: \(n_1=25\), \(\bar{x}_1=42\), \(s_1=14\).
Group 2: \(n_2=30\), \(\bar{x}_2=35\), \(s_2=9\).
Assume unequal variances. Construct a 95% CI for \(\mu_1-\mu_2\).

\[
SE=\sqrt{\frac{14^2}{25}+\frac{9^2}{30}}=3.245
\]
Using Welch \(df\approx38.6\), \(t^*\approx2.023\):
\[
7\pm2.023(3.245)=(0.43,13.57)
\]

The interval is entirely positive, suggesting Group 1 has a higher mean commute time.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Welch t - Food Spending



Group 1: \(n_1=18\), \(\bar{x}_1=96\), \(s_1=22\).
Group 2: \(n_2=22\), \(\bar{x}_2=82\), \(s_2=16\).
Assume unequal variances. Construct a 90% CI for \(\mu_1-\mu_2\).














The 90% CI is approximately \((3.47,24.53)\). Group 1 appears to have a higher mean weekly food spending.

title: STA258
text:
5.4.1.5 Two Means: Assumptions


For all two-sample mean CIs


The two samples are independent.


Each sample is random, or the data come from a randomized design.


Each population is approximately normal, or both samples are large enough for the CLT.




Extra assumption for pooled t


Use the pooled interval only when equal population variances are reasonable.


If the equal-variance assumption is doubtful, use Welch’s interval.

title: STA258
text:
Question


Two independent samples are used to compare average commute times. The population standard deviations are unknown, and the sample standard deviations are noticeably different. Which interval is the most appropriate?




Known-\(\sigma\) two-sample \(z\) interval
Pooled two-sample \(t\) interval
Welch two-sample \(t\) interval
Paired \(t\) interval

title: STA258
STA258
section: Example: Difference of Proportions - Left-Handed Students
text:
Example: Difference of Proportions - Left-Handed Students

Campus 1 has 18 left-handed students out of 120. Campus 2 has 10 left-handed students out of 100.
Construct a 95% CI for \(p_1-p_2\).

\[
\hat p_1=0.1500,\quad \hat p_2=0.1000,\quad \hat p_1-\hat p_2=0.0500
\]
\[
SE=\sqrt{\frac{0.15(0.85)}{120}+\frac{0.10(0.90)}{100}}=0.0443
\]
\[
0.05\pm1.96(0.0443)=(-0.0368,0.1368)
\]

The interval includes 0, so a zero difference in population proportions is plausible.

title: STA258
section: Example: Difference of Proportions - Policy Support
text:
Example: Difference of Proportions - Policy Support



City 1 has 210 supporters out of 500. City 2 has 170 supporters out of 450.
Construct a 90% CI for \(p_1-p_2\).














The 90% CI is approximately \((-0.010,0.095)\). Because 0 is inside, the data do not clearly establish a higher support rate for City 1.

title: STA258
text:
5.4.2.1 Difference of Proportions: Assumptions


Sampling structure


The two groups are independent.


Each sample is random, or the data come from a randomized design.


If sampling without replacement, each sample should be less than 10% of its population.




Large-count condition

For each group, check successes and failures:


\[
x_i \ge 10
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
n_i - x_i \ge 10.
\]

title: STA258
text:
5.4.3 Ratio of Variances

For two normal populations, a confidence interval for \(\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2\) can be written as:
\[
\left(
\frac{s_1^2/s_2^2}{F_{\alpha/2,n_1-1,n_2-1}},
\frac{s_1^2/s_2^2}{F_{1-\alpha/2,n_1-1,n_2-1}}
\right)
\]


This method is sensitive to non-normality. Always check whether normality is a reasonable assumption before trusting an \(F\) interval for variances.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Ratio of Variances - Machines

Machine 1: \(n_1=16\), \(s_1=12\). Machine 2: \(n_2=14\), \(s_2=8\).
Assuming normal populations, construct a 95% CI for \(\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2\).










The 95% CI is approximately \((0.74,6.58)\). Since 1 is inside, equal variances are plausible.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Ratio of Variances - Labs



Lab 1: \(n_1=21\), \(s_1=5.5\). Lab 2: \(n_2=19\), \(s_2=3.8\).
Construct a 90% CI for \(\sigma_1^2/\sigma_2^2\).














The 90% CI is approximately \((0.96,4.51)\). Since 1 is inside, the evidence for different variances is not decisive.

title: STA258
text:
5.4.3.1 Ratio of Variances: Assumptions


Required structure


The two samples are independent.


Each sample comes from a random process or randomized design.




Normality matters here


The \(F\) interval for a variance ratio is sensitive to non-normality.


This condition is more important here than it is for many mean-based intervals.

title: STA258
text:
5.5 Paired Data

For paired observations, reduce each pair to one difference:
\[d_i=M_{2i}-M_{1i}\]
Then construct a one-sample \(t\) interval for the mean difference:
\[
\bar d \pm t_{n-1,\alpha/2}\frac{s_d}{\sqrt n}.
\]



Use paired data when The two measurements come from the same unit, matched units, or before-after observations.


Do not split the pair The pairing is information. Analyze the differences, not the two columns as independent samples.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Paired Data - Tutoring Scores



Ten students take a quiz before and after tutoring. Differences are after minus before:
\[5,2,5,2,4,4,4,4,3,5\]
Construct a 95% CI for the mean improvement.














The 95% CI is approximately \((2.99,4.61)\) points. We are 95% confident that the mean improvement is positive.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Paired Data - Blood Pressure

Twelve patients have blood pressure measured before and after treatment. Let \(d=\) before minus after:
\[6,8,3,10,7,5,9,4,6,8,7,5\]
Construct a 90% CI for the mean reduction.










The 90% CI is approximately \((5.43,7.57)\). Positive values mean the treatment lowers blood pressure on average.

title: STA258
text:
Assumptions for Paired Data

Assumptions


Paired observations: Each pair of values should come from the same unit or from meaningfully matched units.


Independence of pairs: The pairs themselves should be independent of each other.


Normality of differences: The distribution of the paired differences should be approximately normal, especially for small samples.


Random sampling: The sample of pairs should be obtained through a random process or a randomized design.




Important note
The normality condition applies to the differences, not to the original two measurements separately. For larger samples, this condition becomes less critical because of the Central Limit Theorem.

title: STA258
text:
5.6.1 Sample Size for a Mean

If \(\sigma\) is known and desired margin of error is \(E\):
\[
E=z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
n=\left(\frac{z_{\alpha/2}\sigma}{E}\right)^2.
\]
Always round up.

title: STA258
section: Example: Sample Size for a Mean
text:
Example: Sample Size for a Mean

A lab measurement has known \(\sigma=0.0068\) grams per liter. Management wants results accurate within \(E=0.005\) with 95% confidence.
How many repeated measurements are needed?

\[
n=\left(\frac{1.96(0.0068)}{0.005}\right)^2=7.10
\]

Round up: the lab needs \(n=8\) measurements.

title: STA258
section: Example: Sample Size for a Mean
text:
Example: Sample Size for a Mean

A planning value is \(\sigma=22.50\) and the desired margin is \(E=2\).
Find the sample size for 90%, 95%, and 99% confidence.




Level
Critical value
Calculation
Required \(n\)




90%
1.645
\((1.645(22.5)/2)^2=342.41\)
343


95%
1.960
\((1.960(22.5)/2)^2=486.20\)
487


99%
2.576
\((2.576(22.5)/2)^2=839.45\)
840




Higher confidence requires a larger sample size when the desired margin of error stays fixed.

title: STA258
section: 5.6.1 Sample Size for a Mean: Sigma Unknown
text:
5.6.1 Sample Size for a Mean: Sigma Unknown

When \(\sigma\) is unknown, use a planning estimate \(s\) from a pilot study or previous data.
The practical target is:
\[
n=\left(\frac{t_{\alpha/2,n-1}s}{E}\right)^2.
\]


Why this is iterative The \(t\) critical value depends on \(df=n-1\), but \(n\) is what we are trying to find. A common approach is:

Start with the \(z\) approximation.
Use that \(n\) to find a \(t\) critical value.
Recalculate \(n\).
Repeat until \(n\) stops changing.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Sample Size, Sigma Unknown

A pilot study estimates the standard deviation of response time as \(s=12\) seconds. A researcher wants a 95% CI with margin of error at most \(E=5\) seconds.
Find the required sample size using the iterative \(t\) approach.










The sample size stabilizes at \(n=25\), so the researcher needs at least 25 observations.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Sample Size, Sigma Unknown

A pilot study estimates the standard deviation of monthly textbook spending as \(s=18\). A 90% CI is desired with margin of error at most \(E=4\).
Find the required sample size using the iterative \(t\) approach.










The sample size stabilizes at \(n=57\).

title: STA258
text:
5.6.2 Sample Size for a Proportion

For a confidence interval on a population proportion, the margin of error is approximately:
\[
E =
z_{1-\alpha/2}
\sqrt{
\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}
}
\]
Solving for \(n\) gives:
\[
n =
\left(
\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}}{E}
\right)^2
p_0(1-p_0)
\]


The value \(p_0\) is a planning value. If no prior information is available, use \(p_0=0.5\) because it gives the most conservative sample size.

title: STA258
section: Example: Sample Size for a Proportion
text:
Example: Sample Size for a Proportion

A mayoral survey needs to estimate a candidate’s support with 95% confidence and margin of error no greater than 0.03. No prior estimate is available.

\[
n=\left(\frac{1.96}{0.03}\right)^2(0.5)(0.5)=1067.11
\]

Round up: contact at least \(n=1068\) voters.

title: STA258
section: Example: Sample Size for a Proportion
text:
Example: Sample Size for a Proportion

In 2007, 15.6% of people in the USA were not covered by health care insurance. Use \(p^*=0.156\) and \(E=0.03\).
Find the required sample size for 95% and 99% confidence.

\[
n_{95}=\left(\frac{1.96}{0.03}\right)^2(0.156)(0.844)=562.54\Rightarrow563
\]
\[
n_{99}=\left(\frac{2.576}{0.03}\right)^2(0.156)(0.844)=970.97\Rightarrow971
\]

The 99% confidence level requires a larger survey because the critical value is larger.

title: STA258
text:
Question


A two-sample confidence interval for \(p_1-p_2\) is constructed. Which condition checks whether the normal approximation is reasonable?




The two sample means must be equal
The two population variances must be equal
Each group should have enough successes and failures
The sample sizes must be exactly the same

title: STA258
text:
Choosing the Right CI







If the problem asks for…
Use…




one mean and gives \(\sigma\)
one-sample \(z\) interval


one mean and gives \(s\) or raw data
one-sample \(t\) interval


one proportion
one-proportion \(z\) interval


one variance
chi-square interval


difference of means, known \(\sigma_1,\sigma_2\)
two-sample \(z\) interval


difference of means, equal variances
pooled two-sample \(t\) interval


difference of means, unequal/unspecified variances
Welch two-sample \(t\) interval


difference of proportions
two-proportion \(z\) interval


ratio of variances
\(F\) interval


before-after or matched data
paired \(t\) interval on differences

title: STA258
text:
Final Checklist


Before calculating

Identify the parameter.
Check one sample vs two sample vs paired.
Check whether the target is a mean, proportion, or variance.
Pick the reference distribution.



After calculating

Include units when relevant.
Interpret in context.
Check whether 0 or 1 has a special meaning.
For sample size, round up.




One slide takeaway. Confidence intervals are all the same basic idea: estimate the quantity, account for uncertainty, and report a reasonable range of values.

title: STA258
text:
What is Statistical Inference?

Statistical Inference
The aim is to produce estimators of population parameters based on a smaller sample, and to quantify the accuracy of those estimators via a probability statement.
We collect data from a sample → compute statistics → make statements about the population.



Classic inferential question
“How sure are we that the sample mean \(\bar{x}\) is close to the true population mean \(\mu\)?”


Why not measure everyone?
Populations are usually infinite, very large, or expensive to enumerate. Sampling + inference is the practical solution.

title: STA258
text:
4.1 The Normal Distribution



Normal Distribution — \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\)
\[f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \cdot \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\]
for \(-\infty < x < \infty\).
Parameters: mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2 > 0\).


Also called the Gaussian distribution, after Carl Friedrich Gauss (1809). It is symmetric and bell-shaped, completely characterized by \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\).

title: STA258
text:
4.1.1 The Standard Normal Distribution

Standard Normal — \(Z \sim N(0, 1)\)
\[f(z) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \cdot e^{-z^2/2}\]
A special case with \(\mu = 0\) and \(\sigma^2 = 1\). Denoted \(Z\).


Standardising. Any \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) can be converted:
\[Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma} \sim N(0,1)\]
This lets us use a single table (or pnorm()) for any normal distribution.

title: STA258
text:
4.1.2 The Chi-Square Distribution

Chi-Square Random Variable — \(X \sim \chi^2_k\)
If \(Z_1, Z_2, \ldots, Z_k \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} N(0,1)\), then
\[X = \sum_{i=1}^{k} Z_i^2 \sim \chi^2_k\]
The pdf for \(x > 0\) is:
\[f(x; k) = \frac{1}{2^{k/2}\,\Gamma(k/2)}\, x^{k/2 - 1}\, e^{-x/2}\]


The distribution is right-skewed and supported on \((0, \infty)\). As \(k\) increases, it becomes more symmetric. \(E[X] = k\), \(\text{Var}(X) = 2k\).

title: STA258
text:
4.2 Sampling Distributions

Sampling Distribution
The probability distribution of a statistic (such as \(\bar{X}\)) computed from all possible random samples of a given size \(n\) drawn from the same population.



Key idea. \(\bar{X}\) is not a fixed number — it is a random variable. Each new sample of size \(n\) gives a different value of \(\bar{X}\). The sampling distribution describes how those values vary.


Why it matters. Understanding the variability of \(\bar{X}\) from sample to sample is the foundation for confidence intervals and hypothesis tests.

title: STA258
text:
Sampling Distribution of \(\bar{X}\)

Distribution of the sample mean
If \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\) population with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), then:
\[E[\bar{X}] = \mu \qquad \text{Var}(\bar{X}) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\]
The standard error of \(\bar{X}\) is \(\text{SE}(\bar{X}) = \dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\).


Larger \(n\) → smaller SE. Collecting more data shrinks the variability of the sample mean. This is why bigger samples give more precise estimates.

title: STA258
text:
4.3 The Central Limit Theorem

Central Limit Theorem (CLT)
Let \(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n\) be i.i.d. with \(E[X_i] = \mu\) and \(\text{Var}(X_i) = \sigma^2 < \infty\). Then as \(n \to \infty\):
\[\frac{\sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n - \mu)}{\sigma} \;\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}\; N(0,1)\]
Equivalently, for large \(n\): \(\quad \bar{X}_n \;\dot{\sim}\; N\!\left(\mu,\, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)\)


Remarkable. The CLT holds for any parent distribution with finite variance — uniform, exponential, Poisson, or anything else. The shape of \(\bar{X}\) approaches normal as \(n\) grows.

title: STA258
text:
CLT: What “Large \(n\)” Means in Practice


Symmetric distributions Even \(n = 10\)–\(15\) is often enough. The normal approximation kicks in quickly.


Moderately skewed \(n = 30\) is a common rule of thumb. Check with a histogram.


Heavily skewed May need \(n = 50\)–\(100\) or more. The more extreme the skew, the larger \(n\) must be.




Practical consequence. For large \(n\), we can use \(z\)-based confidence intervals and hypothesis tests for \(\mu\) even when the parent distribution is unknown or skewed.

title: STA258

4.4 Convergence in Probability

Convergence in Probability
A sequence \(X_1, X_2, \ldots\) converges in probability to constant \(c\) if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\):
\[\lim_{n\to\infty} P\!\left(|X_n - c| \leq \varepsilon\right) = 1\]
Written \(X_n \overset{p}{\longrightarrow} c\).


Intuition. As \(n\) grows, the probability that \(X_n\) is far from \(c\) shrinks to zero. The sequence settles down near \(c\).

title: STA258
text:
Chebyshev’s Inequality

Chebyshev’s Inequality
For any random variable \(X\) with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), and any \(k > 0\):
\[P(|X - \mu| \geq k) \leq \frac{\sigma^2}{k^2}\]
Equivalently: \(P(|X - \mu| < k) \geq 1 - \dfrac{\sigma^2}{k^2}\)


No distributional assumption. Chebyshev’s inequality holds for any distribution with finite variance. It is the key tool in proving the WLLN.

title: STA258
text:

(b) Use Chebyshev to bound \(P(1 < X < 19)\) from below.
(c) Now suppose \(X\) is actually \(N(10, 9)\). Compute the exact probability \(P(1 < X < 19)\) and compare with the Chebyshev bound.

title: STA258
text:
4.4.2 Weak Law of Large Numbers

Weak Law of Large Numbers (WLLN)
Let \(X_1, X_2, \ldots\) be i.i.d. with \(E[X_i] = \mu\) and \(\text{Var}(X_i) = \sigma^2 < \infty\). Then for any \(\varepsilon > 0\):
\[P\!\left(\left|\bar{X}_n - \mu\right| \geq \varepsilon\right) \longrightarrow 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty\]
Written \(\bar{X}_n \overset{p}{\longrightarrow} \mu\).


This does not say \(\bar{X}_n = \mu\) for large \(n\). It says the probability of being far from \(\mu\) goes to zero. Individual realisations can still deviate.

title: STA258
text:
Proof Sketch: WLLN via Chebyshev



Key steps

\(\text{Var}(\bar{X}_n) = \dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\)
Apply Chebyshev with \(k = \varepsilon\):

\[P\!\left(|\bar{X}_n - \mu| \geq \varepsilon\right) \leq \frac{\sigma^2}{n\varepsilon^2}\]

As \(n \to \infty\), right side \(\to 0\).
Since probability \(\geq 0\), conclude the limit is \(0\). \(\square\)





What does the proof need?

Finite variance \(\sigma^2\)
Independence (for \(\text{Var}(\bar{X}_n) = \sigma^2/n\))
Identical distribution (for common \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\))

The CLT is not required — Chebyshev alone is enough.

Empirical Probability Connection

Empirical Probability from the WLLN
Define indicator \(X_i = \mathbf{1}[\text{event } A \text{ occurs on trial } i]\).
Then \(E[X_i] = P(A)\), and by the WLLN:
\[\bar{X}_n = \frac{\text{number of times } A \text{ occurs}}{n} \;\overset{p}{\longrightarrow}\; P(A)\]


Coin flip. Tossing a fair coin: \(P(\text{heads}) = 0.5\). After many flips, the proportion of heads converges to \(0.5\). This is precisely the WLLN at work.

title: STA258
text:
Chapter Summary


Key Distributions \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) for continuous data; \(\chi^2_k\) for variance; \(t_\nu\) for small-sample means; \(F_{\nu_1,\nu_2}\) for variance ratios.


CLT For i.i.d. data with finite variance, \(\bar{X}_n\) is approximately \(N(\mu, \sigma^2/n)\) for large \(n\), regardless of the parent distribution.


LLN \(\bar{X}_n \overset{p}{\to} \mu\). Sample averages settle near the population mean. Proof uses Chebyshev’s inequality.




One slide takeaway. The CLT and LLN together justify why normal-based inference (confidence intervals, \(t\)-tests) works in practice. Learn the distributions now — everything in Chapters 5+ builds on them.

Chapter Roadmap


6.1 - Logic Null and alternative hypotheses, test statistics, p-values, and decisions.


6.2 - One Sample Tests for one mean, one proportion, and one variance.


6.3 - Two Sample Tests for differences, ratios, and paired data.





Core skill Identify the parameter, then state \(H_0\) and \(H_a\) correctly.


Core tool Use \(Z\), \(t\), \(\chi^2\), and \(F\) reference distributions for p-values.


Core habit State the conclusion in context, without overclaiming a p-value.

title: STA258
text:
6.1 What a Hypothesis Test Does

High Level Idea A hypothesis test uses sample evidence to decide whether there is enough evidence against a claim about a population parameter.



Null hypothesis, \(H_0\) The status quo, no-effect, or no-difference claim.


Alternative hypothesis, \(H_a\) The direction of evidence we are trying to detect.



The test is performed assuming \(H_0\) is true. The p-value measures how unusual the data are under that assumption.

title: STA258
text:
The Five-Step Procedure



1. Choose \(\alpha\). Set the significance level before making the decision.


2. State hypotheses. Use the correct population parameter.


3. Compute statistic. Standardize the estimate with the correct standard error.


4. Find the p-value. Use the tail area that matches \(H_a\).


5. Conclude. Compare to \(\alpha\) and write the conclusion in context.











Step 4 and Step 5 are separate: first calculate evidence, then make the decision.

title: STA258
text:
Choosing the Alternative


Left-tailed \[H_a:\theta < \theta_0\] Use when the research question asks whether the parameter decreased or is smaller.


Right-tailed \[H_a:\theta > \theta_0\] Use when the research question asks whether the parameter increased or is larger.


Two-sided \[H_a:\theta \ne \theta_0\] Use when the research question asks whether the parameter changed in either direction.

title: STA258
text:
P-Value Areas




Left-tailed: \(P(T \le t^*)\) or \(P(Z \le z^*)\).


Right-tailed: \(P(T \ge t^*)\) or \(P(Z \ge z^*)\).


Two-sided: double the matching one-tail area.





Use the dropdown at the top-right of the plot to switch the shaded p-value area between the three alternative hypotheses.

title: STA258
text:
Decision Rule



If p-value \(\le \alpha\) Reject \(H_0\) in favor of \(H_a\).


If p-value \(> \alpha\) Fail to reject \(H_0\).



Careful language Failing to reject \(H_0\) does not prove \(H_0\). It only means the sample does not provide enough evidence against it at the chosen significance level.

title: STA258
text:
Reading Strength of Evidence





p-value range
Textbook language




\(\le 0.001\)
Very strong evidence against \(H_0\)


\(0.001\) to \(0.01\)
Strong evidence


\(0.01\) to \(0.05\)
Evidence


\(0.05\) to \(0.075\)
Some evidence


\(0.075\) to \(0.10\)
Slight evidence


\(>0.10\)
Little or no evidence against \(H_0\)





Statistical significance does not measure practical importance. Pair the p-value with an estimate or confidence interval.

text:

title: STA258
text:
6.2.1.1 One Mean, Known \(\sigma\)

When the population standard deviation is known, use a standard normal reference distribution:
\[
z^*=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}
\]



Reference distribution \(Z\sim N(0,1)\).


Use when Testing a population mean with known \(\sigma\) and an appropriate random/normal-or-large-sample setup.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Coffee Fill Volume



The cafe chain Second Cup advertises that a large iced latte is filled to a target of \(\mu_0=7.2\) oz of base. Customers complain the cups feel light, so quality control pulls a random sample of \(n=40\) cups.
From years of calibration records, the filling machine’s standard deviation is known: \(\sigma=1.1\) oz. The sample mean is \(\bar{x}=6.7\) oz.
Test whether the true mean fill volume has dropped below 7.2 oz at \(\alpha=0.05\).




What we are given

Target mean: \(\mu_0 = 7.2\) oz
Known SD: \(\sigma = 1.1\) oz
Sample: \(n = 40\), \(\bar{x} = 6.7\) oz
Significance level: \(\alpha = 0.05\)



Which test? \(\sigma\) is known, so this is a one-sample \(z\) test with reference distribution \(N(0,1)\).

title: STA258
text:
Coffee Example: Calculation



Hypotheses \[H_0:\mu=7.2 \qquad H_a:\mu<7.2 \quad (\alpha=0.05)\]
Test statistic \[z^*=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}=\frac{6.7-7.2}{1.1/\sqrt{40}}=-2.8748\]
p-value \[\text{p-value}=P(Z\le -2.8748)=0.00202\]















Decision \(0.00202 \le 0.05\), so reject \(H_0\).


Conclusion There is sufficient evidence that the mean fill volume is below 7.2 oz.

For one normal population, test a variance using the chi-square statistic:

6.3.1.1 Two Means: Known \(\sigma_1,\sigma_2\)

When both population standard deviations are known:
\[
z^*=
\frac{(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)-D_0}
{\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1+\sigma_2^2/n_2}}
\]



Usually \(D_0=0\) when testing whether the population means are equal.


Use \(Z\) because the population standard deviations are known.

title: STA258
text:
6.3.1.2 Two Means: Unknown Variances

For unequal or unspecified population variances, use Welch’s two-sample \(t\) test:
\[
t^*=
\frac{(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)-D_0}
{\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2}}
\]



Default Welch is a good default when equal variances are not clearly justified.


Degrees of freedom Software uses the Welch-Satterthwaite approximation.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Workshop Quiz Scores

Two independent tutorial sections try different workshop formats before the same quiz.
Active workshop: 88 91 85 94 89 90 87 92 86 93 89 90
Review workshop: 84 86 82 88 85 83 81 87 84 86
Does the active workshop produce a higher mean quiz score?


Let \(\mu_1\) be the active workshop mean and \(\mu_2\) the review workshop mean. Test \(H_0:\mu_1-\mu_2=0\) against \(H_a:\mu_1-\mu_2>0\).

title: STA258
section: Check in R: Two-Sample t Test
text: Check in R: Two-Sample t Test

title: STA258
STA258
text:
Example: Reminder Texts

A student services office compares sign-up rates with and without reminder texts.
Reminder text: \(142\) sign-ups out of \(360\)
No reminder: \(118\) sign-ups out of \(370\)
Test whether reminder texts increase the sign-up rate.


\[
H_0:p_1-p_2=0,\qquad H_a:p_1-p_2>0
\]

title: STA258
text:
Check in R: Two Proportions









prop.test reports the chi-square form (\(\chi^2=(z^*)^2\)) with p-value \(0.0166\), so there is evidence the daily push notification increases the check-in rate.

title: STA258
text:
6.3.3 Ratio of Variances

For two normal populations, test a ratio of variances with
\[
F^*=\frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2}
\]
using an \(F\) reference distribution with \(n_1-1\) and \(n_2-1\) degrees of freedom.



Normality matters The \(F\) test for variances is sensitive to non-normality.


Two-sided idea Extreme ratios in either direction count as evidence against equal variances.

title: STA258
text:
6.4 Paired Data

For matched pairs or before-after data, first reduce the data to differences:
\[
d_i = \text{new}_i-\text{current}_i
\]
Then run a one-sample \(t\) test on \(\mu_d\).



Not independent groups The two measurements inside a pair are linked.


Reference distribution \(t\) with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom for the differences.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Paired Study Plan Test

Each of 12 students completes a practice set before and after using a new study plan.
Before: 34 29 41 38 36 33 40 31 37 35 39 32
After: 36 31 43 39 38 35 39 34 40 37 41 33
Can we conclude the study plan improves scores?


Use paired differences \(d_i=\text{after}_i-\text{before}_i\) and test \(H_0:\mu_d=0\) against \(H_a:\mu_d>0\).

Question


In the Pomodoro example, why is a paired \(t\) test appropriate?




The two samples have the same mean
The sample size is less than 30
Each student has both before and after scores, so observations are matched within student
Proportion tests cannot use score data

title: STA258
text:
Assumptions: Two Independent Means


Sampling structure


The two samples are independent.


Each sample is random, or the data come from a randomized design.


If sampling without replacement, each sample is less than 10% of its population.




Model condition


Each population is approximately normal, or both sample sizes are large enough for the CLT.


For a pooled test, equal population variances should be reasonable.

title: STA258
text:
Assumptions: Difference of Proportions


Sampling structure


The two groups are independent.


Each sample is random, or the data come from a randomized design.


If sampling without replacement, each sample should be less than 10% of its population.




Large-count condition


Check successes and failures in each group.


At least 10 successes: \(x_i \ge 10\).


At least 10 failures: \(n_i - x_i \ge 10\).

title: STA258
text:
Assumptions: Ratio of Variances


Required structure


The two samples are independent.


Each sample comes from a random process or randomized design.




Normality matters here


The \(F\) test for a variance ratio is sensitive to non-normality.


This condition is more important here than it is for many mean-based tests.

title: STA258
text:
Assumptions: Paired Data


Paired structure


Each pair comes from the same unit, matched units, or a before-after measurement.


The pairs themselves are independent of one another.




Model condition


Analyze the differences \(d_i\), not the two original columns separately.


For small samples, the distribution of differences should be approximately normal.

Choosing the Right Test







If the problem asks for…
Use…




one mean and gives \(\sigma\)
one-sample \(z\) test


one mean and gives \(s\) or raw data
one-sample \(t\) test


one proportion
one-proportion \(z\) test


one variance
chi-square test


difference of means, known \(\sigma_1,\sigma_2\)

pooled two-sample \(t\) test


difference of means, unequal/unspecified variances
Welch two-sample \(t\) test


difference of proportions
two-proportion \(z\) test


ratio of variances
\(F\) test


before-after or matched data
paired \(t\) test on differences

Question


A problem gives raw before-and-after blood pressure measurements on the same 12 patients. Which test should you use?




Two independent sample \(t\) test
One-proportion \(z\) test

title: STA258
text:
Test Statistic Cheat Sheet







Situation
Test statistic




One mean, \(\sigma\) known
\(z^*=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\)


One mean, \(\sigma\) unknown
\(t^*=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt n}\)


One proportion
\(z^*=\frac{\hat p-p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}}\)


One variance
\(\chi^{2*}=\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma_0^2}\)


Two means, \(\sigma_1,\sigma_2\) known
\(z^*=\frac{(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)-D_0}{\sqrt{\sigma_1^2/n_1+\sigma_2^2/n_2}}\)


Two means, pooled \(t\)
\(t^*=\frac{(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)-D_0}{s_p\sqrt{1/n_1+1/n_2}}\)


Pooled variance (\(s_p^2\))
\(s_p^2=\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2+(n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2}\)


Two means, Welch \(t\)
\(t^*=\frac{(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)-D_0}{\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2}}\)


Two proportions
\(z^*=\frac{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}{\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)(1/n_1+1/n_2)}}\)


Ratio of variances
\(F^*=\frac{s_1^2}{s_2^2}\)


Paired differences
\(t^*=\frac{\bar{d}-\mu_{d0}}{s_d/\sqrt n}\)

title: STA258
section: What to Write in a Conclusion
text:
What to Write in a Conclusion


Decision Reject or fail to reject \(H_0\).


Evidence strength Use the p-value to describe how strong the evidence is.


Context Name the population parameter and the direction of the claim.



Good conclusion: “There is sufficient evidence at the 5% level that the mean fill volume for large coffees is below 7.2 oz.”

title: Chapter 3: Descriptive Statistics
text: Slides PDF

title: Chapter 3: Descriptive Statistics
text:
What you’ll learn
By the end of Chapter 3 you’ll be able to:

Write a data set in the standard notation \(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n\) and explain what each symbol stands for.
Compute and interpret the mean, median, and mode as measures of centre.
Compute and interpret the range, variance, standard deviation, and IQR as measures of spread.
Find percentiles and quartiles and use them to describe relative position.
Read skewness and outliers from a histogram or a boxplot.
Use R functions (mean, median, var, sd, summary, quantile, IQR, hist, boxplot) on real data.

title: Chapter 3: Descriptive Statistics
text:
Key ideas

Centre
The mean uses every value and is sensitive to extremes. The median is the middle value and is resistant to outliers. The mode is the most frequent value.


Spread
The range is max minus min — quick but easily distorted by one extreme value. The standard deviation \(s\) is the typical distance from \(\bar{x}\). The IQR \(= Q_3 - Q_1\) is the width of the middle 50% of the data and is resistant to outliers.


Why divide by \(n-1\) for the sample variance?
We use \(\bar{x}\) to estimate the population mean \(\mu\), which costs us one piece of information. Dividing by \(n-1\) corrects for that and makes \(s^2\) an unbiased estimator of the population variance. (Bessel’s correction.)


Position
The \(p^{\text{th}}\) percentile is the value such that \(p\%\) of observations lie below it. Quartiles \(Q_1, Q_2, Q_3\) split the sorted data into four equal-size groups — \(Q_2\) is just the median.


Shape and outliers
A histogram shows the full shape of one variable. A boxplot highlights the five-number summary and flags potential outliers using the \(1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) rule. The longer tail / whisker points in the direction of the skew.


Pair numbers with pictures
A single number rarely tells the whole story. Always report a summary statistic alongside a plot so the shape of the distribution is visible.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: Slides PDF

title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text:
What you’ll learn
By the end of Chapter 1 you’ll be able to:

Distinguish a population from a sample, and identify the unit, observation, and variables in a dataset.
Tell a parameter apart from a statistic — and know which is usually known.
Classify data as quantitative (discrete or continuous) or qualitative (nominal or ordinal).
Recognize common sampling methods and the biases they introduce.
Explain the goal of statistical inference: using a sample to learn about a population, with a measure of uncertainty.

title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text:
Key ideas

Statistics in one sentence
The science of learning from data under uncertainty — moving from what we measured to what we want to know.


Population vs Sample
A population is the full group we want to learn about. A sample is the subset we actually measure. We use the sample to make claims about the population.


Parameter vs Statistic
A parameter (e.g. \(\mu\), \(p\), \(\sigma\)) summarizes the population — usually unknown. A statistic (e.g. \(\bar{x}\), \(\hat{p}\), \(s\)) summarizes the sample — known, and used to estimate the parameter.


Types of Data
Quantitative data are numeric: discrete (counts) or continuous (measured). Qualitative data are categorical: nominal (no order) or ordinal (ordered).


Inference
We collect a sample, calculate a statistic, and use it to estimate an unknown population parameter — always with a measure of uncertainty. This sets up confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, and the rest of the course.

title: Chapter 4: Foundations of Inference
text: Slides PDF

title: Chapter 4: Foundations of Inference
text:
What you’ll learn
By the end of Chapter 4 you’ll be able to:

Describe the Normal, Chi-Square, t, and F distributions and identify when each is used.
Explain what a sampling distribution is and why it is important in statistical inference.
Find the mean and standard error of the sample mean \(\bar{X}\).
Apply the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) to approximate the distribution of sample means.
Understand convergence in probability and interpret the notation \(X_n \overset{p}{\to} c\).
State and apply the Weak Law of Large Numbers (WLLN) to explain why sample averages approach the population mean.

title: Chapter 4: Foundations of Inference
text:
Key ideas

Normal Distribution
The normal distribution is symmetric and bell-shaped, written as \(X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\). The standard normal distribution is the special case \(Z \sim N(0,1)\) and serves as the foundation for many inference procedures.


Chi-Square, (t), and (F) Distributions
The chi-square distribution \(\chi^2_k\) arises from sums of squared standard normal variables. The (t)-distribution \(t_\nu\) is used when the population standard deviation is unknown. The (F)-distribution \(F_{\nu_1,\nu_2}\) is commonly used for comparing variances and in ANOVA.


Distribution Tools in R
Use pnorm and qnorm for normal probabilities and critical values, pchisq and qchisq for chi-square calculations, pt and qt for (t)-distributions, and pf and qf for (F)-distributions.


Central Limit Theorem (CLT)
For large sample sizes, the standardized sample mean is approximately normal: \[
\frac{\sqrt{n}(\bar{X}_n-\mu)}{\sigma}
\overset{d}{\longrightarrow}
N(0,1).
\] This result allows normal-based inference even when the original population is not normal.


Convergence in Probability
The notation \[
X_n \overset{p}{\longrightarrow} c
\] means that as \(n\) grows, the probability that \(X_n\) differs substantially from \(c\) approaches zero.


Weak Law of Large Numbers
The sample mean converges in probability to the population mean: \[
\bar{X}_n \overset{p}{\longrightarrow} \mu.
\] As the sample size increases, sample averages become increasingly stable around the true mean. A proof can be obtained using Chebyshev’s inequality.
