title: STA258
text:
Why Plan the Sample Size?


Too small Low power - real, meaningful effects slip through undetected. The study is wasted.


Too large Wasteful - extra time, cost, and participants for precision you did not need.



Power analysis finds the minimum \(n\) that detects an effect of a given size with a specified probability (power), while holding the Type I rate at \(\alpha\).


To run it you must supply three ingredients: the standard deviation \(\sigma\), the significance level \(\alpha\), and the effect size \(\mu_0-\mu_a\) you want to detect.

title: STA258
text:
The Sample-Size Idea



1. Cutoff from \(H_0\). Write \(\bar{x}_*\) using the null mean and \(z_\alpha\).


2. Cutoff from the target power. Write the same \(\bar{x}_*\) using the alternative mean and \(z_\beta\) (the \(z\) giving the desired power).


3. Set the two expressions equal and solve for \(n\). Round up to the next whole observation.



One-sided sample-size formula \[n=\left(\frac{(z_\alpha+z_\beta)\,\sigma}{\mu_0-\mu_a}\right)^{2}\] where \(z_\beta\) is the standard-normal value matching the target power.

title: STA258
section: Example: Detecting a Lift in Daily Active Minutes
text:
Example: Detecting a Lift in Daily Active Minutes


A product team’s app currently averages \(\mu_0=100\) daily active minutes. A new onboarding flow is believed to lift engagement. With \(\sigma=14\), they want power \(0.60\) to detect a true mean of \(\mu=103\). What is the smallest \(n\)? \[H_0:\mu=100 \qquad H_a:\mu>100 \qquad (\alpha=0.05)\]


Cutoff under \(H_0\) \(\;\bar{x}_*=100+1.645\cdot\tfrac{14}{\sqrt n}\)
Cutoff for power 0.60 \(\;P(Z>-0.25)\approx 0.60 \;\Rightarrow\; \bar{x}_*=103-0.25\cdot\tfrac{14}{\sqrt n}\)
Equate and solve \[100+1.645\cdot\tfrac{14}{\sqrt n}=103-0.25\cdot\tfrac{14}{\sqrt n}
\;\Rightarrow\; n=\left(\frac{(1.645+0.25)\cdot 14}{103-100}\right)^2\approx 78.2 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{n=79}\]

\(n\approx 78.2\), so a minimum of 79 observations guarantees power of at least 0.60. (Using the rounded \(z_\beta=0.25\) from the table gives the same answer.)

title: STA258
text:
Example: Vending-Machine Coffee


A campus vending machine advertises \(225\) ml cups (\(\sigma=7\) ml). You suspect it pours less. How many cups must you sample to reach power \(0.80\) against a true mean of \(\mu=223\) ml? (Target: \(P(Z<0.84)\approx0.80\), so \(z_\beta=0.84\).) \[H_0:\mu=225 \qquad H_a:\mu<225 \qquad (\alpha=0.05)\]


Equate the two cutoffs \(\;225-1.645\tfrac{7}{\sqrt n}=223+0.84\tfrac{7}{\sqrt n}\)
Solve for \(n\) \[n=\left(\frac{(1.645+0.84)\cdot 7}{225-223}\right)^2\approx 75.6 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{n=76}\]


A minimum of 76 cups delivers the desired 0.80 power against a 2 ml shortfall.

title: STA258
section: Power for a Proportion: Same Logic
text:
Power for a Proportion: Same Logic

For a one-sided test of \(p\), the rejection cutoff uses the null standard error, but power is computed with the alternative standard error:
\[\hat p^{\,*}=p_0 \mathbin{\substack{+\\[-4pt]-}} z_\alpha\sqrt{\tfrac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}, \qquad
\text{power}=P\!\left(\hat p \text{ in reject region}\;\middle|\; p=p_a\right)\]


Which sign on \(z_\alpha\)?








Test
Cutoff \(\hat p^{\,*}\)
Reject when




\(H_a:p<p_0\)
\(p_0-z_\alpha\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}\)
\(\hat p<\hat p^{\,*}\)


\(H_a:p>p_0\)
\(p_0+z_\alpha\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}\)
\(\hat p>\hat p^{\,*}\)





Three steps, same as the mean

Find the cutoff \(\hat p^{\,*}\) from \(p_0\) and \(z_\alpha\).
Standardize that cutoff under \(p=p_a\) using \(\text{SE}_a\).
The tail area past it is the power.

title: STA258
text:
How Many Viewers for Power 0.80?


Keep \(H_0:p=0.90\), \(H_a:p<0.90\), true \(p=0.85\), \(\alpha=0.05\). Set power \(=0.80\) (\(z_\beta=0.8416\)) and equate the two cutoff expressions: \[0.90-1.645\sqrt{\tfrac{0.90(0.10)}{n}}=0.85+0.8416\sqrt{\tfrac{0.85(0.15)}{n}}\]


\[\sqrt n=\frac{1.645\sqrt{0.09}+0.8416\sqrt{0.1275}}{0.05}=\frac{0.4935+0.3005}{0.05}\approx 15.88\] \[n\approx 252.2 \;\Rightarrow\; \boxed{n=253}\]

title: STA258
text:
General Power Formulas


Right-tailed, \(H_a:\mu>\mu_0\) \[\text{Power}(\mu_a)=\pi(\mu_a)=P\!\left[\,Z\ge z_\alpha+\frac{\sqrt n\,(\mu_0-\mu_a)}{\sigma}\right]\]


Left-tailed, \(H_a:\mu<\mu_0\) \[\text{Power}(\mu_a)=\pi(\mu_a)=P\!\left[\,Z\le -z_\alpha+\frac{\sqrt n\,(\mu_0-\mu_a)}{\sigma}\right]\]


Two-sided, \(H_a:\mu\ne\mu_0\) \[\text{Power}(\mu_a)=1-P\!\left[-z_{\alpha/2}+\frac{\sqrt n\,(\mu_0-\mu_a)}{\sigma}\le Z\le z_{\alpha/2}+\frac{\sqrt n\,(\mu_0-\mu_a)}{\sigma}\right]\]

title: STA258
text:
What You Need to Know


Standard deviation \(\sigma\) - the spread of the variable being measured.


Significance level \(\alpha\) - the fixed Type I error rate you are willing to tolerate.


Effect size \(\mu_0-\mu_a\) - the smallest difference worth detecting.



With data in hand it is more common to report a p-value than a fixed reject/not-reject decision: it measures the strength of evidence against \(H_0\) and leaves the action up to each reader.

title: Chapter 7: Statistical Power
text:
What you’ll learn
By the end of Chapter 7 you’ll be able to:

Compute the power of a \(z\) test against a specific alternative mean or proportion.

Identify the three ingredients (\(\sigma\), \(\alpha\), effect size) you must know before planning a study.

title: Chapter 7: Statistical Power
text:
Key ideas

What Power Means
The power of a test is the probability of correctly rejecting \(H_0\) when a particular alternative is true: \(\text{Power}=P(\text{reject }H_0\mid H_0\text{ false})\). High power means the test reliably detects real effects.


Two Kinds of Error
A Type I error rejects a true \(H_0\) (probability \(\alpha\)); a Type II error fails to reject a false \(H_0\) (probability \(\beta\)). Power is exactly \(1-\beta\), so shrinking \(\beta\) raises power.


What Drives Power
Power increases with the effect size, the sample size \(n\), and the significance level \(\alpha\), and decreases with variability \(\sigma\). Since \(n\) and \(\alpha\) are under your control, sample size is the main planning lever.


Computing Power
Translate the rejection rule into a cutoff on the data scale using the null distribution, then assume the alternative is true and find the probability of landing in the rejection region. That area is the power.


Planning the Sample Size
Setting a cutoff under \(H_0\) equal to a cutoff under the desired power gives \(n=\big((z_\alpha+z_\beta)\sigma/(\mu_0-\mu_a)\big)^2\). Smaller effects and lower variability tolerance demand larger samples; always round \(n\) up.

title: STA258
text:
Sweetness: Cutoff to Power



Rejection Rule One-sided \(\alpha=0.05\) gives \(z_{\text{crit}}=1.645\). On the \(\bar{x}\) scale (since \(\sigma\) is known): \[\bar{x}_*=0+1.645\cdot\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{10}}\approx 0.520 \;\Rightarrow\; \text{reject if } \bar{x}>0.520\]


Find the Power Assume \(\mu=1.1\) is true and find \(P(\bar{x}>0.520)\): \[\text{power}=P\!\left(Z>\tfrac{0.520-1.1}{1/\sqrt{10}}\right)=P(Z>-1.83)=\mathbf{0.9664}\]












A 96.6% chance of correctly detecting \(\mu=1.1\). Since power \(=1-\beta\), the green and red areas add to 1: \[\text{power}=1-\beta=1-0.034=0.966\]

text:
7.3 Using Power to Determine Sample Size


Too small Low power - real, meaningful effects slip through undetected. The study is wasted.


Too large Wasteful - extra time, cost, and participants for precision you did not need.



Power analysis finds the minimum \(n\) that detects an effect of a given size with a specified probability (power), while holding the Type I rate at \(\alpha\).


To run it you must supply three ingredients: the standard deviation \(\sigma\), the significance level \(\alpha\), and the effect size \(\mu_0-\mu_a\) you want to detect.

What you’ll learn
By the end of Chapter 8 you’ll be able to:

State the one-way ANOVA model and explain what each term represents.
Partition the total variation into between-group (treatment) and within-group (error) sums of squares.
Build an ANOVA table and compute the \(F\) statistic.

title: Chapter 8: Analysis of Variance
text:
Key ideas

Comparing Several Means
ANOVA extends hypothesis testing to three or more group means at once. The null hypothesis is that all group means are equal; the alternative is that at least one differs.


Partitioning Variation
The total variation \(\text{SSTotal}\) splits into the variation between groups (SSTr, the treatment effect) and the variation within groups (SSE, the error): \(\text{SSTotal}=\text{SSTr}+\text{SSE}\).


The F-Statistic
Dividing each sum of squares by its degrees of freedom gives mean squares, and \(F=\text{MSTr}/\text{MSE}\) compares between-group to within-group variation. A large \(F\) is evidence against equal means.


Multiple Comparisons
A significant \(F\) says the means are not all equal, but not which ones. Pairwise methods such as Fisher’s LSD (higher power) and the Bonferroni adjustment (controls the experiment-wise error rate) locate the differences.

title: STA258
text:
Why ANOVA?


Purpose
Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) is used to compare several population means at once.
Instead of running many separate two-sample tests, ANOVA begins with one global test.



Question
Do all groups have the same population mean?
\[
k \ge 3
\]
groups are being compared.


Null hypothesis
The population means are all equal:
\[
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_k
\]


Alternative hypothesis
At least one population mean is different:
\[
H_a:\text{not all }\mu_i\text{ are equal}
\]



Key idea
ANOVA tells us whether there is evidence that at least one mean differs.
If ANOVA rejects (H_0), then pairwise comparisons can ask which means differ.

title: STA258
text:
One-Factor ANOVA Model


Textbook model
For observation \(j\) in group \(i\):
\[
Y_{ij}=\mu+\tau_i+\epsilon_{ij},
\qquad
\epsilon_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma^2),
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\tau_i=0
\]
Here, \(Y_{ij}\) is the response value for observation \(j\) in group \(i\). The constraint \(\sum_{i=1}^{k}\tau_i=0\) makes \(\mu\) the overall population mean and uniquely defines the treatment effects.


Equivalent form
Since the population mean for group \(i\) is
\[
\mu_i=\mu+\tau_i,
\]
the same model can be written as
\[
Y_{ij}=\mu_i+\epsilon_{ij},
\qquad
\epsilon_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma^2)
\]


Meaning of the notation

\(\mu\): overall population mean
\(\tau_i\): treatment effect for group \(i\)
\(\epsilon_{ij}\): random error for observation \(j\) in group \(i\)
\(\mu_i=\mu+\tau_i\): population mean of group \(i\)



Intuition
Each observation is modeled as
\[
\text{response}
=
\text{group mean}
+
\text{random error}.
\]
So ANOVA asks whether all group means are equal:
\[
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_k
\]
or whether at least one group mean differs.

title: STA258
text:
Sources of Variation

ANOVA works by splitting variation into two pieces: variation within groups and variation between groups.



Within groups: error variation
\[
SSE=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(n_i-1)S_i^2
\]
This is residual variation inside the groups.


Between groups: treatment variation
\[
SSTr=\sum_{i=1}^{k} n_i(\bar X_i-\bar X)^2
\]
This captures how group means differ from the overall mean.



The ANOVA \(F\) statistic becomes large when between-group variation is large relative to within-group error variation.

title: STA258
text:
Total Variation and Decomposition


Total variation
Total variation measures how far all observations are from the overall mean.
\[
SSTotal=
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}
(X_{ij}-\bar X)^2
\]


What ANOVA compares
ANOVA compares variation between group centers to variation inside the groups.
\[
\text{between-group variation}
\qquad \text{vs.} \qquad
\text{within-group variation}
\]


Decomposition identity
Total variation splits into treatment variation plus error variation:
\[
SSTotal=SSTr+SSE
\]


Intuition
If group means are close together, \(SSTr\) is small.
If at least one group mean is far away, \(SSTr\) becomes larger.


Big picture
ANOVA asks whether the between-group variation is large compared with the within-group error variation.

text:
The ANOVA Table


ANOVA table structure



Source

Total
\(n-1\)
\(SSTotal\)






\[
SSTotal=SSTr+SSE
\]
\[
F^*=\frac{MSTr}{MSE}
\]

The p-value comes from the right tail of the (F) distribution.


Mean square rule
A mean square is a sum of squares divided by its degrees of freedom:
\[
MS=\frac{SS}{df}
\]
So in one-way ANOVA:
\[
MSTr=\frac{SSTr}{k-1},
\qquad
MSE=\frac{SSE}{n-k}
\]


Degrees of freedom
The degrees of freedom split the same way as the sums of squares:
\[
n-1=(k-1)+(n-k)
\]
Treatment variation uses (k-1) df, and error variation uses (n-k) df.


Test statistic and p-value
The ANOVA test statistic is
\[
F^*=\frac{MSTr}{MSE}
\]
Under \(H_0\),
\[
F^*\sim F_{k-1,\;n-k}
\]
The p-value is the right-tail area.

title: STA258
text:
Hypothesis Test and Reference Distribution



Hypotheses:
\[
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_k
\]
\[
H_a:\text{at least one }\mu_j\text{ is different}
\]


Test statistic
\[
F^*=\frac{MSTr}{MSE}
=
\frac{SSTr/(k-1)}{SSE/(n-k)}
\]
Under \(H_0\):
\[
F^*\sim F_{k-1,n-k}
\]




The ANOVA p-value is always a right-tail probability.


Large \(F^*\) means the treatment variation is large compared with error variation.

title: STA258
text:
Assumptions of ANOVA


Assumptions


Observations are independent.




Error terms, or residuals, are Normal.




All groups have the same population variance:

\[
\sigma_1^2=\sigma_2^2=\cdots=\sigma_k^2=\sigma^2.
\]



Common variance estimate
The common variance is estimated using the Mean Squared Error from ANOVA:
\[
\hat{\sigma}^2=MSE
\]

title: STA258
text:
What If ANOVA Rejects?


Global ANOVA result
ANOVA tests whether all population means are equal:
\[
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_k
\qquad \text{vs.} \qquad
H_a:\text{at least one mean is different}
\]



Important limitation
Rejecting \(H_0\) tells us that not all means are equal.
It does not tell us which specific groups differ.


Follow-up question
After a significant ANOVA result, we ask:
\[
\text{Which means are different?}
\]


Pairwise comparisons
For three groups:
\[
\mu_1-\mu_2,\qquad
\mu_1-\mu_3,\qquad
\mu_2-\mu_3
\]
With \(k\) groups:
\[
m=\binom{k}{2}
\]



Next step
Use pairwise confidence intervals to compare specific group means: first Fisher’s LSD, then Bonferroni.

title: STA258
text:
Pairwise Confidence Intervals


General idea
After ANOVA rejects, compare two population means using an interval for \(\mu_i-\mu_j\):

\[
(\bar{x}_i-\bar{x}_j)
\pm
t^*
\sqrt{
MSE\left(\frac{1}{n_i}+\frac{1}{n_j}\right)
}
\qquad
\text{where } \hat{\sigma}^2=MSE
\]




Fisher’s LSD
Use the ordinary two-sided critical value:
\[
t^*=t_{1-\alpha/2,\;n-k}
\]
This gives narrower intervals, so it has more power to detect differences.
It is less conservative when many pairs are compared.


Bonferroni
First count the number of pairwise comparisons:
\[
m=\binom{k}{2}
\]
Then use the adjusted critical value:
\[
t^*=t_{1-\alpha/(2m),\;n-k}
\]
This gives wider intervals.


Decision rule
A pair is declared different when the interval for \(\mu_i-\mu_j\) does not contain 0.
If the interval contains 0, the pair is not clearly different.
So the whole method is:
\[
\text{interval avoids }0
\Rightarrow
\text{different}
\]

Bonferroni

\[

\sqrt{

\left(
\frac{1}{n_i}+\frac{1}{n_j}
\right)
}
\]
Conclude two means differ if:
\[
|\bar x_i-\bar x_j|>LSD
\]

Bonferroni vs. Fisher: Decision Guide


Fisher LSD

Easier to calculate.
Higher power.
Does not control experiment-wise Type I error.



Bonferroni

Controls experiment-wise Type I error.
Uses wider intervals.
Has lower power and higher Type II error risk.

Final Checklist


Before calculating ANOVA

Identify the response variable.
Identify the grouping variable.
State \(H_0:\mu_1=\cdots=\mu_k\).

After calculating ANOVA

Fill in df, SS, MS, and \(F^*\).

title: Chapter 8: Analysis of Variance
text:
STA258: Statistics with Applied Probability
University of Toronto Mississauga






8.1 - ANOVA idea Use one test to compare several population means.


8.2 - Variation split Separate total variation into treatment variation and error variation.


8.3 - F-test Build the ANOVA table and use a right-tailed F distribution.





8.4 - Assumptions Normal residuals, equal population variance, and independent observations.


8.5 - Comparisons After a significant ANOVA, use Fisher’s LSD or Bonferroni.


8.6 - R workflow Use oneway.test(), aov(), and pairwise.t.test().







Analysis of Variance, or ANOVA, is used to compare several population means.
Suppose there are \(k\) groups, usually with \(k \ge 3\).



Bad habit Run many separate two-sample tests.


ANOVA habit Start with one global test:
\[H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_k\]


Interpretation If the global test rejects, then at least one population mean differs.



ANOVA does not immediately tell us which mean is different. That comes later with pairwise comparisons.








The textbook model is:
\[
Y_{ij}=\mu+\tau_i+\epsilon_{ij},
\qquad
\epsilon_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma^2)
\]
where \(Y_{ij}\) is observation \(j\) in group \(i\).


Meaning of the pieces

\(\mu\): overall mean
\(\tau_i\): treatment effect for group \(i\)
\(\epsilon_{ij}\): random error
\(\mu+\tau_i\): mean of group \(i\)





Equivalent form:
\[
Y_{ij}=\mu_i+\epsilon_{ij},
\qquad
\epsilon_{ij}\sim N(0,\sigma^2)
\]
where \(\mu_i\) is the population mean of group \(i\).


Each observation in the same group is modeled as having the same population group mean, plus random error.

Notation

\(\bar X_i\): sample mean of group \(i\)
\(S_i^2\): sample variance of group \(i\)
\(n_i\): sample size of group \(i\)



Total sample size:
\[n=n_1+n_2+\cdots+n_k\]
Overall sample mean:
\[
\bar X=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}X_{ij}
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{k}n_i\bar X_i
\]








ANOVA works by splitting the total variation into two pieces.



Within groups: error variation
\[
SSE=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(n_i-1)S_i^2
\]
This measures residual variation inside the groups.


Between groups: treatment variation
\[
SSTr=\sum_{i=1}^{k}n_i(\bar X_i-\bar X)^2
\]
This measures how far group means are from the overall mean.



If group means are far apart compared with the within-group noise, the ANOVA F statistic becomes large.








Total variation:
\[
SSTotal=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}(X_{ij}-\bar X)^2
\]


Decomposition identity
\[
SSTotal=SSTr+SSE
\]




ANOVA asks whether the between-group variation is large relative to the within-group variation.


If all group means are similar, \(SSTr\) should be small.
If at least one group mean is far away, \(SSTr\) gets larger.

#| autorun: false
anova_summary <- function(n, xbar, s2) {
  k <- length(n)
  N <- sum(n)

  grand <- sum(n * xbar) / N
  SSTR <- sum(n * (xbar - grand)^2)
  SSE <- sum((n - 1) * s2)

  df1 <- k - 1
  df2 <- N - k

  MSTR <- SSTR / df1
  MSE <- SSE / df2
  Fstar <- MSTR / MSE
  pval <- pf(Fstar, df1, df2, lower.tail = FALSE)

  data.frame(grand, SSTR, SSE, MSTR, MSE, Fstar, pval)
}

out <- anova_summary(
  n = c(6, 6, 6),
  xbar = c(1.33, 2.50, 2.67),
  s2 = c(1.87, 2.30, 1.47)
)

round(out, 3)

Assumptions


Observations are independent.


Error terms, or residuals, are Normal.


All groups have the same population variance: \(\sigma_1^2=\sigma_2^2=\cdots=\sigma_k^2=\sigma^2\).




The common variance is estimated using the Mean Squared Error from ANOVA:
\[
\hat\sigma^2=MSE
\]


This is why the denominator of the F statistic is \(MSE\): it estimates the shared within-group variance.








ANOVA’s alternative is broad:
\[
H_a:\text{at least one mean is different}
\]
So after rejecting \(H_0\), we still need to ask:
Which mean or means are different?




Pairwise comparisons
Compare the means in pairs.
For three groups:

\(\mu_1\) vs. \(\mu_2\)
\(\mu_1\) vs. \(\mu_3\)
\(\mu_2\) vs. \(\mu_3\)



Number of comparisons:
\[
\binom{k}{2}
\]








For comparing two group means after ANOVA, use intervals for:
\[
\mu_i-\mu_j
\]



Fisher’s LSD
\[
(\bar x_i-\bar x_j)\pm
t_{1-\alpha/2,n-k}
\sqrt{MSE\left(\frac{1}{n_i}+\frac{1}{n_j}\right)}
\]
More power, but does not control experiment-wise Type I error.


Bonferroni
\[
(\bar x_i-\bar x_j)\pm
t_{1-\alpha/(2m),n-k}
\sqrt{MSE\left(\frac{1}{n_i}+\frac{1}{n_j}\right)}
\]
where \(m=\binom{k}{2}\). Controls experiment-wise Type I error.














Method
Main idea
Tradeoff




Fisher LSD
Uses ordinary pairwise confidence intervals after ANOVA
Higher power, but does not control experiment-wise Type I error


Bonferroni
Makes each pairwise interval wider by adjusting for \(m\) comparisons
Controls experiment-wise Type I error, but has lower power




Least significant difference
\[
LSD=t_{1-\alpha/2,v}
\sqrt{MSE\left(\frac{1}{n_i}+\frac{1}{n_j}\right)}
\]
Conclude two means differ if:
\[
|\bar x_i-\bar x_j|>LSD
\]

#| autorun: false
means <- c(Classic = 20, Streak = 25, Leaderboard = 30)
n <- c(6, 6, 6)
names(n) <- names(means)

MSE <- 2
v <- 15
alpha <- 0.05
m <- choose(length(means), 2)

pairs <- combn(names(means), 2)

out <- lapply(seq_len(ncol(pairs)), function(a) {
  i <- pairs[1, a]
  j <- pairs[2, a]

  diff <- means[i] - means[j]
  se <- sqrt(MSE * (1/n[i] + 1/n[j]))

  data.frame(
    pair = paste(i, "-", j),
    diff = diff,
    LSD_low = diff - qt(1 - alpha/2, v) * se,
    LSD_up = diff + qt(1 - alpha/2, v) * se,
    Bonf_low = diff - qt(1 - alpha/(2*m), v) * se,
    Bonf_up = diff + qt(1 - alpha/(2*m), v) * se
  )
})

round(do.call(rbind, out), 2)

Use Fisher LSD when…

You want a simpler post-ANOVA comparison.
You accept higher experiment-wise Type I error risk.
Power is the priority.



Use Bonferroni when…

You want stronger control of experiment-wise Type I error.
You have many pairwise comparisons.
You are okay with wider intervals and lower power.




Textbook takeaway: Bonferroni corrects the multiple-comparisons problem; Fisher LSD is easier and more powerful but does not maintain the same experiment-wise error control.

3
6

Before calculating ANOVA

Identify the response variable.
Identify the grouping variable.
State \(H_0:\mu_1=\cdots=\mu_k\).
Check independence, Normal errors, and equal variance.



After calculating ANOVA

Fill in df, SS, MS, and \(F^*\).
Use the right-tail F p-value.
Reject only when the p-value is small.
If ANOVA rejects, use pairwise comparisons to find which means differ.




One slide takeaway. ANOVA compares several means by asking whether between-group variation is large compared with within-group error variation.

title: STA258
text:
ANOVA Hypothesis Test


Hypotheses
The null hypothesis says all population means are equal:
\[
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_k
\]
The alternative says at least one population mean differs:
\[
H_a:\text{not all }\mu_i\text{ are equal}
\]


Reference distribution
Under \(H_0\), the test statistic follows an \(F\) distribution:
\[
F^* \sim F_{k-1,\;n-k}
\]
Numerator df:
\[
k-1
\]
Denominator df:
\[
n-k
\]


Test statistic
The ANOVA test statistic is
\[
F^*
=
\frac{MSTr}{MSE}
=
\frac{SSTr/(k-1)}{SSE/(n-k)}
\]
It compares between-group variation to within-group error variation.


P-value
The ANOVA p-value is the area to the right of \(F^*\).
\[
p\text{-value}=P(F_{k-1,\;n-k}\ge F^*)
\]
Large \(F^*\) values give evidence that the group means differ more than expected from random error alone.

title: STA258
text:
Example: Event Flyers and Sign-Ups


Problem
A student club studies fictional data from a community event promotion.
For each day:

\(x=\) flyers posted around campus
\(y=\) new sign-ups in tens

Data:
\[
x: 1,\;2,\;3,\;4,\;5
\]
\[
y: 1,\;1,\;2,\;2,\;4
\]
Test whether the slope differs from 0.


Hypotheses and conclusion
\[
H_0:\beta_1=0,
\qquad
H_A:\beta_1\ne0
\]
The reference distribution is \(t_3\).
Since the p-value is about 0.035, reject \(H_0\) at the 5% level.
There is evidence of a positive linear relationship.


Calculation
From least squares:
\(\hat y=-0.100+0.700x\), \(SSE=1.100\), \(S_{xx}=10.000\), \(n=5\).

1. Estimate the error variance
\(s^2=\dfrac{SSE}{n-2}=\dfrac{1.100}{5-2}=\dfrac{1.100}{3}=0.3667\)
\(s=\sqrt{0.3667}=0.6055\)

2. Standard error of the slope
\(SE(\hat\beta_1)=\dfrac{s}{\sqrt{S_{xx}}}
=\dfrac{0.6055}{\sqrt{10}}
=0.1915\)

3. Test statistic
\(t=\dfrac{\hat\beta_1-0}{SE(\hat\beta_1)}
=\dfrac{0.700}{0.1915}
=3.656\)
\(df=n-2=5-2=3\)

4. Confidence interval for the slope
\(95\%\ CI:\ \hat\beta_1\pm t_{0.975,3}SE(\hat\beta_1)\)
\(=0.700\pm3.182(0.1915)\)
\(=(0.091,\;1.309)\)

s

SE(\hat{\beta}_1)

\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
t
&=\frac{\hat{\beta}_1-0}{SE(\hat{\beta}_1)}

=23.926,\\[-1pt]
df
&=n-2
=8-2
=6.

\[
\begin{aligned}
95\%\ CI
&:\quad
\hat{\beta}_1\pm t_{0.975,6}SE(\hat{\beta}_1)\\[-1pt]
&=
1.038\pm2.447(0.043)\\[-1pt]
&=
(0.932,\;1.144).

text:
9.1.1 Least Squares Method

A residual is the difference between an observed data point and a fitted value from the regression model:
\[
e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i.
\]
It is the vertical distance from the observed value to the fitted line.












If \(e_i > 0\), the point is above the fitted line.
The model underpredicted the response.


If \(e_i < 0\), the point is below the fitted line.
The model overpredicted the response.

title: STA258
text:
ANOVA as a Prediction Problem


Main idea
ANOVA compares two prediction rules: one that ignores the group and one that uses the group.



Ignore group information
Predict every observation using the overall mean:
\[
\widehat X_{ij}=\bar X
\]
Total prediction error:
\[
SSTotal=
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}
(X_{ij}-\bar X)^2
\]
All observations are treated as coming from one common center.


Use group information
Predict observation \(j\) in group \(i\) using its group mean:
\[
\widehat X_{ij}=\bar X_i
\]
Remaining prediction error:
\[
SSE=
\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j=1}^{n_i}
(X_{ij}-\bar X_i)^2
\]
Each group is allowed to have its own center.



Improvement from using groups
The variation explained by group membership is the reduction in prediction error:
\[
SSTr=SSTotal-SSE
\]
If this improvement is large compared with the within-group error, the ANOVA (F) statistic becomes large.

Setup
Use the ANOVA output:
\[
MSE=4.90,
\qquad
v=n-k=18-3=15
\]
There are
\[
m=\binom{3}{2}=3
\]
pairwise comparisons.
Since each group has size 6, we use Bonferroni intervals for each difference in population means.


Calculation
First find the sample means:
\[
\bar{x}_1=\frac{19+20+21+23+24+25}{6}=22
\]
\[
\bar{x}_2=\frac{24+25+26+28+29+30}{6}=27
\]
\[
\bar{x}_3=\frac{26+27+28+29+30+31}{6}=28.5
\]
For Bonferroni intervals at the family-wise \(5\%\) level:
\[
t^*
=
t_{1-\alpha/(2m),\,15}
=
t_{1-0.05/(2\cdot3),\,15}
=
t_{0.99167,\,15}
=
2.69
\]
Since \(n_1=n_2=n_3=6\),
\[
SE
=
\sqrt{
MSE\left(\frac{1}{n_i}+\frac{1}{n_j}\right)
}
=
\sqrt{
4.90\left(\frac16+\frac16\right)
}
=
1.28
\]
\[
ME=t^*(SE)=2.69(1.28)=3.44
\]
Now find each sample mean difference:
\[
\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2=22-27=-5.00
\]
\[
\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_3=22-28.5=-6.50
\]
\[
\bar{x}_2-\bar{x}_3=27-28.5=-1.50
\]
Therefore the Bonferroni intervals are:
\[
\mu_1-\mu_2:\ -5.00\pm3.44=(-8.44,\,-1.56)
\]
\[
\mu_1-\mu_3:\ -6.50\pm3.44=(-9.94,\,-3.06)
\]
\[
\mu_2-\mu_3:\ -1.50\pm3.44=(-4.94,\,1.94)
\]

text:
Fisher’s LSD


Idea
Fisher’s LSD is used after ANOVA rejects.
It compares two group means using the pooled error estimate from ANOVA:
\[
MSE
\]
It is more powerful, but it does not control the experiment-wise Type I error rate.


Textbook formula
For each pair:
\[
(\bar{x}_i-\bar{x}_j)
\pm
t_{\alpha/2,v}
\sqrt{
MSE
\left(
\frac{1}{n_i}+\frac{1}{n_j}
\right)
}
\]
where:
\[
v=n-k
\]
A pair differs if its interval does not contain 0.

title: STA258
text:
Fisher’s LSD: The Idea


Least Significant Difference
Fisher’s LSD compares two group means after the overall ANOVA test has rejected \(H_0\).
For a pair of groups \(i\) and \(j\), we compare the observed mean difference:
\[
\bar{x}_i-\bar{x}_j
\]



Shared error estimate
Use the pooled within-group variation from ANOVA:
\[
MSE
\]
This estimates the common variance \(\sigma^2\).


Ordinary t critical value
Fisher’s LSD uses:
\[
t^*=t_{1-\alpha/2,\;n-k}
\]
The degrees of freedom come from the ANOVA error row.


LSD cutoff
When group sizes are \(n_i\) and \(n_j\):
\[
LSD=
t^*
\sqrt{
MSE\left(\frac{1}{n_i}+\frac{1}{n_j}\right)
}
\]



How to decide
If
\[
|\bar{x}_i-\bar{x}_j|>LSD,
\]
then the pair is declared different. Fisher’s LSD is powerful, but it is less conservative when many pairwise comparisons are made.

title: STA258
text:
Bonferroni: Why Adjust?


The issue
After ANOVA rejects, we may compare many pairs of means.
Each pairwise comparison has a chance of making a Type I error, so doing many comparisons increases the chance of making at least one false discovery.



1. Count comparisons
With \(k\) groups, the number of pairwise comparisons is
\[
m=\binom{k}{2}.
\]
For example, if \(k=4\),
\[
m=\binom{4}{2}=6.
\]


2. Experiment-wise error
If each comparison uses error rate \(\alpha\), then the chance of making at least one Type I error is
\[
\alpha_E=1-(1-\alpha)^m.
\]
As \(m\) increases, \(\alpha_E\) increases.


3. Bonferroni correction
To keep the overall error rate controlled, Bonferroni uses a smaller per-comparison level:
\[
\frac{\alpha}{m}.
\]
For a two-sided interval, this gives
\[
t^*=t_{1-\alpha/(2m),\;n-k}.
\]



Key idea
Fisher’s LSD is more powerful, but it does not control the experiment-wise Type I error rate.
Bonferroni is more cautious: it uses wider intervals to protect against making false discoveries across many pairwise comparisons.

title: STA258
text:
6.3.2 Hypothesis Tests on Two Proportions

When testing \(H_0:p_1-p_2=0\), pool the sample proportions under the null and use the test statistic
\[
\hat p=\frac{x_1+x_2}{n_1+n_2},
\qquad
z^*=\frac{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}{\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)(1/n_1+1/n_2)}}
\]
which, under \(H_0\), follows the standard normal reference distribution \(Z\sim N(0,1)\).



Reference distribution \(z^*\sim N(0,1)\).


Use when Comparing two population proportions from independent samples, with enough successes and failures in each group.

text:
Download Speeds: Calculation



Hypotheses \[H_0:\mu_A-\mu_B=0 \qquad H_a:\mu_A-\mu_B>0 \quad (\alpha=0.05)\]
Test statistic \[z^*=\frac{(\bar{x}_A-\bar{x}_B)-0}{\sqrt{\sigma_A^2/n_A+\sigma_B^2/n_B}}=\frac{86-79}{\sqrt{12^2/40+15^2/45}}=2.387\]
p-value \[\text{p-value}=P(Z\ge 2.387)=0.0085\]















Decision \(0.0085 \le 0.05\), so reject \(H_0\).


Conclusion There is evidence Provider A’s mean download speed is higher than Provider B’s.

title: STA258
text:
Two Fertilizers: Calculation



Hypotheses \[H_0:\mu_A-\mu_B=0 \qquad H_a:\mu_A-\mu_B\neq 0 \quad (\alpha=0.05)\]
Pooled variance \[s_p^2=\frac{(n_A-1)s_A^2+(n_B-1)s_B^2}{n_A+n_B-2}=\frac{8(0.274^2)+9(0.221^2)}{17}=0.0612\]
Test statistic \[t^*=\frac{\bar{x}_A-\bar{x}_B}{s_p\sqrt{1/n_A+1/n_B}}=\frac{4.10-3.63}{0.2475\sqrt{1/9+1/10}}=4.13\]
p-value \[\text{p-value}=2\,P(T_{17}\ge 4.13)=0.0007\]















Decision \(0.0007 \le 0.05\), so reject \(H_0\).


Conclusion There is strong evidence the two fertilizers give different mean yields.

title: STA258
text:
Active Recall vs Rereading: Calculation



Hypotheses \[H_0:\mu_1-\mu_2=0 \qquad H_a:\mu_1-\mu_2>0 \quad (\alpha=0.05)\]
Test statistic (no pooling) \[t^*=\frac{\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2}{\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2}}=\frac{86.92-84.60}{\sqrt{2.392^2/12+1.506^2/10}}=2.76\]
p-value \[\text{p-value}=P(T_\nu\ge 2.76)=0.0062,\qquad \nu\approx 18.8\]















Decision \(0.0062 \le 0.05\), so reject \(H_0\).


Conclusion There is evidence active recall produces a higher mean quiz score than rereading.

text:
Push Notifications: Calculation



Hypotheses \[H_0:p_1-p_2=0 \qquad H_a:p_1-p_2>0 \quad (\alpha=0.05)\]
Sample and pooled proportions \[\hat p_1=\tfrac{142}{360}=0.394,\quad \hat p_2=\tfrac{118}{370}=0.319,\quad \hat p=\tfrac{142+118}{360+370}=0.356\]
Test statistic \[z^*=\frac{\hat p_1-\hat p_2}{\sqrt{\hat p(1-\hat p)(1/n_1+1/n_2)}}=\frac{0.0756}{0.0354}=2.13\]
p-value \[\text{p-value}=P(Z\ge 2.13)=0.0166\]















Decision \(0.0166 \le 0.05\), so reject \(H_0\).


Conclusion There is evidence the daily push notification increases the check-in rate.

text:
Interactive: Watch Power Climb with \(n\)
Use the dropdown to change the sample size for the bottling test (\(\mu_0=300\), \(\mu_a=299\), \(\sigma=3\), left-tailed \(\alpha=0.05\)). As \(n\) grows, both curves sharpen, they separate more cleanly, and the green power area past the cutoff expands.









Same 1 ml shortfall, same \(\alpha\), only \(n\) changes: power rises from \(\approx 0.20\) at \(n=6\) to \(\approx 0.83\) at \(n=60\). That is why sample size is your main planning lever.

title: STA258
text:
Chapter Summary


Global ANOVA test Test
\[
H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2=\cdots=\mu_k
\]
against the claim that not all population means are equal.


Variation and the F statistic ANOVA splits total variation into treatment and error variation, then compares them using
\[
F^*=\frac{MSTr}{MSE}.
\]


After rejection A significant ANOVA result says at least one mean differs. Use Fisher’s LSD or Bonferroni intervals to determine which pairs differ.




One slide takeaway. Use ANOVA for the global question first, then use adjusted pairwise comparisons to investigate specific mean differences.
